speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. In view of the unplanned drop of our dollar which fell below 96 cents this morning in relation to the United States dollar, a five cent drop in a week, would the minister indicate if news reports in New York are correct when they state that the Bank of
[Mr. MacKay.J
Canada has used substantial amounts of our United States dollar reserves to support the Canadian dollar within the last three or four days, to prevent the Canadian dollar from falling to still lower levels? If so, would the minister indicate to what extent reserves have been so used?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: FINANCE
subsubtopic: DROP IN VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-SUPPORT BY BANK OF CANADA-USE OF UNITED STATES DOLLAR RESERVES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is the policy of the Bank of Canada to intervene from time to time with price movements of the dollar, in order to maintain an orderly market. The state of the foreign exchange fund is reported on after the end of each month and the current state will be reported on at the end of this month. It has also not been the policy to disclose on a day to day basis the particular amount of intervention. For that reason I would prefer not to comment to the House at this point, although this information will be available within the month.

DROP IN VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR- EFFECT ON INVESTMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Is the minister not concerned that the reduced confidence in the Canadian dollar would reflect itself also in reduced confidence among investors in Canada, both international and Canadian investors, with deep economic consequences for Canada resulting from a reduction in the rate of investment including an increase in unemployment?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: DROP IN VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR- EFFECT ON INVESTMENT
speechtext: Several possible conclusions can be drawn from the drop in value of the Canadian dollar. It has been anticipated, both at home and abroad, for some time that there would a readjustment downward in the Canadian dollar when the heavy calendar of borrowings, particularly by provincial institutions, was finished this year. To the extent that there has been the expected readjustment downward, I think one might expect that foreign investors, seeing an expected stability in the dollar rate, might not be deterred from investing in Canada. On the other hand, of course, I think we must be concerned about the possible impact of political events in Canada, and indeed about the rate of inflation on the continued confidence that foreign investors will have in this country. I will be conscious of that in any policy I put forward.

subtopic: DROP IN VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-MEASURES TO RESTORE CONFIDENCE
DROP IN VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-MEASURES TO RESTORE CONFIDENCE
speechtext: In view of the sharp decline of the dollar-and I hope the minister is right in suggesting, as he seemed to be suggesting, that this will be brought about quite quickly, although there is no reason that we can see here to believe that at the moment-does the minister intend to take any new initiatives, in the light of this display of lack of confidence in the Canadian economy, to restore confidence in the economy and indeed in the integrity of Canada-and by "initiatives" I assure you I am not implying the suggestion that Ed Schreyer and I should be invited to join the government-or whether he intends to stand pat, as he indicated he was going to do when he last made a statement in the House a week or so ago?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: DROP IN VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-MEASURES TO RESTORE CONFIDENCE
speechtext:
It is not
evident to me that any initiatives that might be taken-for example, by stimulating the domestic economy and stimulating the domestic demand-would necessarily produce a more favourable reception of the Canadian dollar or Canadian investments abroad. It seems to me that probably the most effective policy to be pursued is that to which the government has given priority, that is to reduce the rate of inflation. That continues to be the policy.

One of our essential rights or obligations as members of parliament is the monitoring of spending by the government or by agencies inextricably connected to the government over which the government has responsibility and authority. That, Mr. Speaker, is the issue that I think is involved or that I will argue is involved in my question of privilege.
The former auditor general, Mr. Henderson, wrote a letter to the Prime Minister Vh years ago in which he outlined some very questionable financial practices of Polysar Corporation. He did so instead of doing what, in my opinion, he ought to have done, which was to have brought the matter to the attention of this House. He is an officer of this House, and his obligation is to report such activities to the House of Commons and not to the Prime Minister. That was not done and he exercised that judgment at that time.
In a letter dated March 27, 1973, the Prime Minister, in writing to the former president of the Treasury Board, agreed that such practices raised at least the possibility of embarrassment and also intimated that they were possibly illegal. In the letter to the former president of the Treasury Board he suggested that the minister at that time should "organize a discussion on the question" with three other specified ministers of the Crown. The Prime Minister concluded his letter with the specific request that this matter be "given immediate consideration", and urged the minister to report back to him with his conclusions or suggested course of action, presumably.
My question of privilege is that we, as members of parliament, would not have learned of this very serious possibility of financial wrongdoing or possibly illegal financial wrongdoing-and not simply moral wrongdoing-had not the former auditor general brought this matter out into the open, into the public, last week. The question of privilege I raise is twofold in nature: the first aspect is that the Prime Minister ought to have acted immediately to have the situation described to him by the former auditor general thoroughly investigated. Then he ought to have ensured that such inappropriate activity as he thought was possible-and turned out to be the case-was stopped or, if the activity that he requested be investigated turned out to be illegal, that ought to have been stopped as well.
In fact, instead of ensuring that such action was completed, the Prime Minister simply sent a letter VA years ago and did nothing else in the interim. We would not be discussing it here in the House of Commons under a question of privilege today had it not been for the former auditor general deciding last week that he had to raise the matter, not in a letter to the House of Commons or to any minister of the Crown or the Prime Minister but that he had to release it to the press.

The second aspect of my question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, is that in my view the Prime Minister, as a member of this House and as the head of the cabinet which derives its authority from having support in this House of Commons, had an obligation not only to investigate and correct such financial wrongdoing, if it existed, but had a further obligation to report back either at the time or after it was cleared up to all members of the House of Commons so that we would know about it. This, too, was not done.
That, Mr. Speaker, is my question of privilege. If you should rule that I have a prima facie case, I am prepared to move that this matter be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections and that the Prime Minister and the former auditor general be asked to appear as witnesses.

Let me come to the issue which faces the Chair: Is there a question of privilege? Usually, a question of privilege is raised because someone has done something wrong. It is a little easier, then, to see it. The question of privilege raised by my leader, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) relates to the fact that something was not done, and the something which was not done was an act of omission on the part of two persons: first, Mr. Maxwell Henderson in his failure to report to parliament things he had discovered and about which he wrote to the Prime Minister; and, second, the Prime Minister in his failure to let the House know what Mr. Henderson had told him.
The point of our having read all this correspondence over and over again is to establish the fact that Mr. Henderson knew what was wrong and wrote about it to the Prime Minister, who then knew it too. He said in the paragraph quoted by my hon. friend from Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) that he was not reporting it to parliament, for certain reasons which we question. At any rate, there were two persons-Mr. Henderson, who was responsible to parliament, and the Prime Minister, who was also responsible to parliament. Both knew certain facts about which parliament should have been told, and their failure to tell parliament what was going on interfered with our right and our capacity to do
Privilege-Mr. Broadbent
our job. That is my point: the failure to do certain things interfered with our right and capacity to do our job.

A reference to it was just made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. At any rate, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre concluded his remarks by saying that the two people who wronged parliament should be brought before the standing committee: that is my recollection.

subtopic: MR. BROADBENT-GOVERNMENT'S HANDLING OF AUDITOR GENERALS' REPORTS
speechtext:
The standing committee. The fact is that there is one question here, and that is the ability of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts-and one standing committee is as good as another, in my view, in this respect-to carry out an investigation. One standing committee seeks to investigate this matter, and there is some question outstanding at the present time as to whether or not its terms of reference are broad enough to enable it to do so. If not, there has been a clear commitment, in my opinion, and unequivocal commitment by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen), that the terms of reference ought to be broadened permit that investigation. Therefore that question appears to me to be entirely separate from the question of privilege.
This leaves on its own the question of privilege which was raised, and raised very seriously, by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby. The question is, it seems to me, that the Auditor General brought something to the attention of the Prime Minister of the day, about 3'A years ago, rather than bringing it to the attention of parliament. Certainly, had he wished to bring it to the attention of parliament he was sufficiently experienced at that time to have done so; I do not think there is any doubt about that. He, having brought it to the attention of the Prime Minister, and the matter having relationship to a Crown corporation as opposed to a govern-

ment department, is it possible that failure on his part to bring that to the attention of parliament could then place upon the Prime Minister of the day not only an obligation to do so but such an obligation that his failure to do so would offend the privileges of this House as we know them to be under the classic definition of privilege?
I can only conclude by saying that for me to begin to broaden the classic definition of parliamentary privilege to that extent would be out of all keeping with the definition as we have always understood it. Again, this is not to suggest for one minute that the matter is not serious. It is obviously serious. The Prime Minister himself said-and he is certainly, I think, making an accurate prediction-that this is not going to be the end of the matter.
I must say 1 am guided to some extent by the commitment made that if the public accounts committee is not able to look into this, it certainly ought to be able to, and that if its terms of reference are not broad enough to look into it, they ought to be attended to. This being the case, it would be difficult for me to attempt to extend the umbrella of privilege to cover this matter, one which obviously has been taken into account by the House, the House having demonstrated its will to do so in some way, shape or form. Therefore, I cannot entertain this as a question of privilege.

Mr. Speaker, I understand the motion is debatable. I do not rise to oppose the motion, but I am in a somewhat embarrassing situation. The subject matter of this letter, together with the revelations made public last Friday, came at a time when the steering committee of the public accounts committee did not have an opportunity to discuss the matter. So what I say now, I say as an individual member of the House and of the public accounts committee.
I point out, Mr. Speaker, that we are getting into a rather extraordinary field of investigation for a standing committee of the House, one quite foreign to the usual activities of a standing committee, specifically the public accounts committee. We would not now be dealing with a subject matter that is within the control of the government, within the control even of this House, indeed within the control of a Crown corporation. We will be dealing, hopefully, with the production of witnesses and the production of documents which would entail the releasing of those matters to the committee by a commercial organization that has been removed even one further sphere away than the rather insular attitude of Crown corporations of this government.
I can see absolutely nothing wrong with the actual terms of reference, but my purpose in standing before you today, sir, is to plead for a situation that may well come about in the future. I refer to the fact that if, for instance, a foreign-based corporation which now has very nebulous ties with this government and this parliament refuses to give the committee the full access which I am sure the committee will demand, then we will have to come back to this House to have the terms of reference perhaps even further widened in order to give us subpoena powers to produce documents.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES RESTRAINT ACT

speechtext: The House resumed, from Monday, November 29, consideration of the motion of Mr. Andras that Bill C-19, to amend or repeal certain statutes to enable restraint of government expenditures, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates; and the amendment thereto of Mr. Holmes (p. 1393).

subtopic: GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES RESTRAINT ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to continue my remarks on Bill C-19, the restraint of government spending, and the amendment by a member of this party which, in effect, suggests that the bill should be read the second time six months hence. It is my belief that this amendment is very timely in that it will give the government six months in which to bring in a more comprehensive bill. I would urge hon. members to consider it seriously and vote in favour of it. Perhaps the government does not require six months. I think it could manage to do this much faster than that. In the many excellent speeches we have heard during the debate, particularly those of my colleagues, many areas that were not covered have been pointed out. It has become quite clear that the bill as it now stands is quite cosmetic and deals mainly with the transfer of payments and the indexing of family allowances. It is only a one-shot deal, mainly window-dressing.
There is, in fact, a great deal of inefficiency and empirebuilding in this government. This bill should really go to the fundamental cutting of government expenditures, indicating clearly what this government intends to do in the future. The taxpayers of this country want the fat trimmed from government spending. The taxpayers are aware of the large increase in government spending over the past few years, and they know that this has been almost out of control since 1971. The people want to activate the conscience of this government and its cabinet ministers. They realize the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) really does not have a conscience, but they wonder if this is true of the rest of the cabinet. The Minister of Transport is not here today, but he is one who likes to fly around in his Jetstar, spending money and arrogantly trying to defend such expenditure.
The transportation system of this country requires a lot of upgrading and overhaul. The Minister of Transport has flown into my riding and told the people engaged in the fruit industry there that if it is cheaper to send their fruit to eastern Canada via United States railways, that is what they should do. That is not the kind of action that will alleviate the unemployment problem in Canada. The Minister of Transport knows full well that those engaged in the fruit industry have contracted for piggyback cars with the railway companies and must utilize those cars to the fullest extent if they are to live
November 30, 1976

up to the contracts. This has boxed them in with Canadian railways to a great extent.
The minister is also aware of the fact that the Canadian railways, I suppose as a result of his running around talking about the concept of user-pay, intend to increase their freight rates on British Columbia apples by 17 per cent. This will put the growers in the position of paying 2 cents a pound, or SI a box more than via U.S. railways. We have to utilize the Canadian railways, and that is as it should be, but when representations are made to the minister he says he cannot do anything about the 17 per cent increase. When representations are made to the Anti-Inflation Board we are told it can do nothing about the situation, and when representations are made to the Canadian Transport Commission we are told it can do nothing-yet 17 per cent is higher than that allowed labourers, and higher than set out in the Anti-Inflation Board guidelines. This form of transportation is being allowed this kind of a percentage increase, while the Minister of Transport flies around the country spending money with great abandon, doing very little about transportation problems in Canada. This is the kind of thing the people want cut back, and this is the area where the fat can be trimmed. Such action would indicate that the government is sincere about restraint in government spending.
We know, as should this government, that small businesses form the backbone of this country. We also know we have an unemployment problem. This problem could be alleviated by making small businesses stronger so that they, in turn, could put people to work. To accomplish this we must have reductions in income taxes paid by small businesses. We must put our resources into those areas where we can put the people to work. This will be done only if the government comes to its senses and realizes it must restrain government spending.
We know very well that this government takes far too great a percentage of the gross national product. This means that the government's spending is out of line. The government spends much more, and much more quickly, than it should. This is the reason I fully support the amendment that the bill be read six months hence, to give the government an opportunity to take a real look at government spending and bring forward something that is comprehensive and meaningful in respect of stopping the government spending that is going on in Canada today.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES RESTRAINT ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the issue before the Elouse is restraint in government spending. I think it is important at the outset of my comments to point out that we on this side of the House would support any serious intent by this government to restrain the amount of spending. Bill C-19, however, does not meet this objective. Moreover, it causes most significant harm to the Canadian society. It is with that perspective in mind that I am pleased to speak again on the amendment that has been put forward by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes) to the effect that this bill not be read at the present time but that it be read six months hence.
Restraint of Government Expenditures
We are now in a situation where the government of Canada spends $42 billion. If we look at some of the clauses of Bill C-19 we see things such as the indexing of family allowances. This will mean, in effect, that those in the higher income brackets will not receive family allowances-which does not bother me-but it will also mean that by the indexing, the burden will be borne by families with lower incomes. In my remarks I intend to demonstrate clearly that this government has numerous options by which effectively to practice restraint without even bringing such legislation before the House.
I think the fact that it has brought in Bill C-19 shows lack of imagination and lack of ability on the part of the government to face up to the fact that it has so grossly overspent in many areas that no bill is necessary in order to bring about restraint. The bill is intended to repeal certain statutes to enable restraint of government expenditures. The hypocrisy of the bill is that the restraint fails to meet the test of significance. While the government may be claiming a $1.5 billion restraint program by Bill C-19, the fact is that by the time one has finished reading the bill and doing the mathematical calculations in respect of what the bill actually does, one finds that, in effect, it does not save $1.5 billion but probably saves a few million. What happens is that the rest of it is a shift in cost, as I will demonstrate later in my speech. As an example, some ports will be closed because of the "at and east" policy which the government is talking about retracting. People will be laid off jobs. That is no saving. The saving that takes place there will be merely shifted to unemployment insurance or to a job-creation charge at the other end of the spectrum. So in reality we cannot talk about this bill saving anywhere near $1.5 billion: at least half of that amount will be a shifting of the cost from one pocket to another pocket of the government.
I have the privilege to speak on the amendment in respect of a six-month hoist, but I would rather speak in favour of a lifetime burial of Bill C-19. No one will deny the need for the government of the day to practice restraint, but the government does not need a bill enshrined in parliament to achieve that objective. If the government of the day were sincere about restraint, we might ask why it did not listen to and act in concert with the Auditor General in respect of his recommendations. If the government were truly interested in restraint, it would have taken action by this date clearly to enunciate its intention to establish a comptroller general. That, of course, has not been the practice of the government. That act in itself would have restrained far more money than would Bill C-19 or any similar measure.
We could also ask, if this government truly intends to restrain its fiscal spending, why it has not brought down a new budget which truly talks about restraint and has truth built within it. If the government really wanted to do something about restraint, it could talk about replacing the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) with a person who practices the concept of user-pay. Also, if the government were really interested in restraint it could drop the delaying tactics of appointing a royal commission on federal fiscal accountability.

November 30, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures
It seems to me that nothing could underscore more the hypocrisy of the government than the fact that it has received, in succession, two auditor generals' reports that condemn the government for its lack of fiscal management-and then, after receiving those reports from two different auditors general, the government says, in effect, that all it will do is appoint a royal commission. I should like to read into the record two short paragraphs from an editorial in the Edmonton Journal of Wednesday, November 24, 1976, which quite accurately expresses my opinion of what is really the purpose in calling for a royal commission. The editorial states:
Announcing a royal commission-in this case, to study the criticized uncontrolled spending-is one of the oldest political tricks. It buys time and permits inaction, under the excuse that a report on the subject is being prepared.
But this time, if the opposition and the people of Canada buy this old line, they will do themselves and the nation a very great disservice. The situation, as Auditor General J. J. Macdonell said, is "critically serious," and after deteriorating for the past 15 years remedies are needed quickly.
Mr. Speaker, if the government is sincere in any attempt at restraint, we will have very quickly to see rise up from the opposite side of the House some action which will indicate that there is something in the Auditor General's report which requires attention and consideration. If we look at another way in which government spending could be restrained, then I think it is time to tell the Prime Minister's private advisers to get off the disguised welfare system and get on with doing a job. They should get on with the job of doing something which is different than that being done for which we already have advisers in the various departments.
We could give the same message to the multitude of private consultants who hang like albatrosses around the necks of each and every department of government. The fact of the matter is that a department of government is established to give counsel to the minister, and I think it is foolishness that the Canadian taxpayers should have to pay, at the rate they do, the exorbitant costs involving private consultations both with the PMO and the various departments of government.
If we sincerely want to trim the $42 billion the government spends of our gross national product, we should bring about significant measures. We should bring about measures which would cause a reduction of taxes and would increase productivity in big and small businesses in this country. As long as we are talking about measures dealing with only millions of dollars-and I do not want to underestimate the importance of the word "millions"-we are not talking about real restraint, and we will not be until this government can demonstrate that it is restraining in terms of billions of dollars, because that is the kind of budget it has laid before the people of Canada.
The word "hoist" implies raising up, but this bill should be buried. I would like to consign Bill C-19 to its final resting place with the following arguments: first, there has been no demonstrative effort to control federal government expenditures. We might ask what might have been done to ensure some restraint. Let us consider some of the anomalies which occur within this bill in an effort to demonstrate that it fails in
terms of significance, that it contains a measure of harm, and that it is discriminatory of what I consider the two outer regions of this country.
The removal of the "at and east" rate is another case of removing a support system from the economies of the prairies and the Atlantic regions. The removal of those rates would cause farmers in the west to sing the song, "Oh, where have all the flour mills gone?" Only two decades ago my constituency was dotted with flour mills. Because of transport policies and this attempt to remove the "at and east" support system, the flour industry is being centralized more and more away from where products are grown. This government wonders why the country appears to be on shaky ground and why some regions have difficulty talking about a unified and solid Canada. There seems to be a direct plan by the government to cause stresses which are unnecessary by favouring a centralization policy, not only in terms of power in Ottawa but in terms of controlling where economic centres and secondary industries are developed.
Virtually all the flour mills on the prairies are extinct. Every industrialized country which has a flour-milling industry has a subsidy for that industry. For government members to talk about removing the "at and east" subsidies is to be unaware of the facts and to be discriminatory of the Atlantic provinces, particularly the ports of Saint John and Halifax. It is definitely discriminatory of the grain producing districts in the western provinces. The government wishes to remove the "at and east" subsidy in the name of restraint, but this bill not only fails to restrain in a significant way but also hampers the movement of grain products from one part of the country to another.
This is another case of padding for central Canada. The removal of the "at and east" subsidy will likely destroy the grain handling aspect of the Saint John and Halifax ports but will have almost no effect on the port of Montreal. Is that a saving? If we take jobs away from one area under the mask of restraint, will there not be more cost by way of increases in unemployment insurance, and will there not be a loss of human dignity and manpower in terms of people being employed in meaningful work? What about the psychological depression which is bound to take place as a result of some of the offshoots and spinoffs of this bill? If unamended, it would cause a higher rate of unemployment in certain regions.
The government talks about restraint and expropriates
88,000	acres for a federal airport called Mirabel. The estimated loss for next year is $46 million. It is hypocrisy to bring in a bill like Bill C-19 when we do not have a new budget and when we do not have a government which is really restraining itself in terms of billions of dollars.
The staff of the Post Office has increased 50 per cent in one decade. When we consider the growth of government spending, we wonder if hon. members opposite can even spell the word "restraint". The government terminated Information Canada with restraint in mind, only to find that expenditures by all other departments rose 16.5 per cent, for a total additional cost of $14,786,000. When we consider that, we can see the

November 30, 1976

implications of Bill C-19. Just a year ago the government said it would do away with Information Canada and there would be a big saving. Then we found that the information costs in all departments increased in excess of $14 million. That is exactly what will happen with regard to other aspects of Bill C-19.
Hon. members of this side of the House are 100 per cent in favour of a sincere restraint program. It is hypocrisy to bring in a bill in an attempt to appeal to the Canadian people with regard to restraint when the fact of the matter is that in every way this bill simply shifts money from one pocket to another and there is no serious intention to restrain government spending. There is no serious effort to cut back personal income tax, which is now at its highest rate in history, and there is no serious intention to stimulate small, middle-sized and big business.
In recent budget debate speeches the word "restraint" has been echoed in nearly every paragraph. But how does the government practice restraint? It does so by increasing capital construction costs by $85 million for the years 1976 and 1977. That is some restraint! Capital expenditures will grow from $546 million to $800 million in the years 1976 and 1977. What is the sense of having a restraint bill when the government practices absolutely the opposite? To a Liberal, doubling costs is considered restraint, if hon. members are serious about restraint, they should be asking themselves such questions as this: have the personnel in the Post Office doubled in the last eight years from 39,180 people to 60,524 people and, if so, why does the Post Office provide only half the service it once did?
Mr. Speaker, I should like to bring to the attention of the House the fact that in 1895 Van Horne moved a division of troops from Ottawa to Winnipeg in ten days when three sections of the railway were still not completed. Just yesterday a constituent wrote me and wanted to know why it took 29 days for a first-class letter to come from Ontario to Alberta- and that follows a doubling of the staff of the Post Office over the last eight years. Yet the government has the audacity to say there is going to be some kind of restraint as a result of Bill C-19.
If there is to be restraint, let us have a budget that shows restraint and cutbacks in a way that is best for the Canadian people. We could send those letters from Ontario to Alberta better by horse and buggy, and I mean that literally. The service of the Post Office, which cost $263 million eight years ago, now costs $850 million in salaries alone. Time and time again members of parliament get letters complaining about the very slow and inadequate service. In the short time that I have been here, I know that the number of people who are dissatisfied with this postal service is growing. We have twice the staff and half the service.
The Unemployment Insurance Commission doubled its staff in the past eight years, and while that created more jobs for the commission, unemployment rose from 400,000 to 850,-000-again, a doubling of staff with half the result. It is important to underscore that if the federal government is truly
Restraint of Government Expenditures intent on a program of restraint, it behooves it either to act immediately upon the recommendations of the Auditor General or to introduce a budget forthwith that would have in it restraint that would be significant to the Canadian taxpayer. Without such stimulus we simply carry on with the same rituals.
That can be clearly demonstrated by analysing what has happened over the years in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. While I have a good deal of sympathy for the plight of our native people, and I believe it is the role and responsibility of government to show concern and interest in them, the fact is that the bureaucracy of the department has grown to such an extent that if we were to allocate to the Indian families the money it costs to run the department, every family would receive $17,135. I do not suggest that we should give every Indian family $17,000 and do away with the department, Mr. Speaker, but that is what the bureaucracy costs. I think we should reverse this kind of thinking.
Bill C-19 provides that the family allowance will be frozen, but the allowance is taxed anyway-yet the government claims it is practising restraint. Restraint practised on the backs of the people on low income in this country is something that should be challenged not only by members of this House but by all Canadians. I think nothing could more clearly demonstrate that Bill C-19 is improperly before the House than the statement of the Auditor General at page 3 of the Conspectus, where he said:
In the majority of the Crown corporations audited by the Auditor General, financial management and control is weak and ineffective. Moreover, co-ordination and guidance by central government agencies of financial management and control practices in these Crown corporations are virtually non-existent.
If this government really wants to save money and to increase the saving from the millions to billions, then let it be done in one fell swoop. Let us do away with Petro-Can and save $5.5 billion, and not waste our time with an insincere bill that does not restrain, that is not a stimulus to the economy and that will have the effect of creating more activity in the small business community but will not reduce personal income tax. This is simply a shadow-mask with the intention of making the people believe that the government is doing something about restraint. The truth of the matter is that in almost any department no restraint is taking place. The Auditor General underscored that when he said, again, at page 3 of the Conspectus:
I am deeply concerned that, on the evidence of the two-year examination carried out by the audit office, parliament-and indeed the government-has lost or is close to losing effective control of the public purse.
We do not need Bill C-19 in order to gain control of the public purse, yet that is probably one of the most devastating comments that could be made in a thorough study of the financial operation of a government in the history of Canada. To claim that Bill C-19 is in some way going to bring about a restraint and financial improvement aspect is simply reducing the Canadian mentality to its lowest common denominator. I think the government has to recognize that Canadians are more intelligent than that. They know what the government is

November 30, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures about, and they know it has an obligation to bring out a budget and to follow the Auditor General's recommendations in such a way that there will be a "felt" restraint program. By "felt", I mean that the Canadian people will see a difference in how the economy is operated and there will be a stimulus for business throughout all sectors of the economy.
Crown corporations have been mentioned, Mr. Speaker. I would recommend that all members of the government make an effort to study Crown corporations with a view to removing as many of them as possible. As the Auditor General points out at page 4:
Based on the study of the systems of departments, agencies and Crown corporations audited by the Auditor General, financial management and control in the government of Canada is grossly inadequate. Furthermore, it is likely to remain so until the government takes strong, appropriate and effective measures to rectify this critically serious situation.
Little can be said about Bill C-19 other than it is a mask held before the Canadian people in an effort to try to disguise the issues of the day. It is a mask held up to try to pretend the government is doing something about restraint. It is a mask for the claim that they are removing $1.5 billion from federal spending. In almost every instance this is either detrimental to the poor people of this country or the poor regions of this country. Sometimes it just shifts the cost from one department to another.
The "at and east" rates and subsidies would be removed by Bill C-19. If this is carried out, it will undoubtedly cause high employment in the ports of Saint John and Halifax, so it is no saving at all. It merely represents a shift of dollars from a subsidy on grain movement to unemployment insurance and to larger manpower staffs which will be needed to deal with the discontent of those in the regions who are alienated from the present centralist government.
It is time to come to grips with the real issue confronting us, the lack of control over this country's financial management. You cannot bring our finances under control simply by restraining expenditures in a few areas, such as family allowances, the "at and east" subsidies and those aspects with which Bill C-19 seeks to deal. If the government is truly serious about restraint, it can show it only if it introduces a new budget. That budget should go to the heart of government spending by freezing the hiring of more employees for the federal government.
The government should commit itself to restricting its own growth until such time as its fiscal policies are in order. Until that is done, this government has no business putting forward Bill C-19. Therefore, I feel privileged in asking the House to adopt the amendment requesting a six months' hoist with respect to second reading of Bill C-19. I hope that during that six-month period the government will take genuine action in terms of analysing its fiscal policies, will look into Crown corporations which are operating in such a terribly inefficient way, and introduce a budget that will significantly reduce the proportion of the gross national product which the government appropriates.

Hon. members will recall that less than a decade and a half ago the two senior levels of government took about 29 per cent of the gross national product for government expenditures. Today, that figure has risen to 42 per cent of the gross national product for the two senior levels of government. Obviously, if one looks at the converse side of the question, the more governments take for their own expenditures, the less remains available for the private sector of society. One must therefore ask government supporters if they, as Liberal members of parliament, believe in the free enterprise system and if they concur in the practice whereby the government takes an ever larger proportion of the gross national product. If they concur in that practice, then obviously they deny the proposition that there should be freedom of thought and of practice for all individuals in society, for they think that the government should be in charge of the economy and not the people, not the grass-roots of the country.
A second danger arises from the government's appropriating an ever larger share of the gross national product. The present government practice suggests that it is in favour of weaker provinces and a stronger federal government, a practice which threatens the fabric of confederation by alienating the far-flung regions of this country-the regions far removed, geographically, from the centre. It should be noted that in the outer regions of Canada there is far greater discontent over bread and butter issues and less confidence in the federal government than was demonstrated even in the November 15 election in the province of Quebec.
If the government shows no sense of fair play and equity, if it persists in bringing before this House bill after bill jeopardizing transportation policies affecting the prairies and the Atlantic regions, in due course the hair on the back of the necks of the people in those regions will rise and you will see demonstrations and actions which will be far more significant than those simply based on differences of language and culture. People live by bread and butter and react when their livelihood is threatened. People in the regions do not look kindly on the present government's practice of taking an ever larger share of the gross national product, of pulling money in from the regions and dumping it in the central area known as the Golden Triangle.
I hope all hon. members will recognize that by recommending the six-month hoist we are not saying that we do not intend to restrain government expenditure. Rather, it is a request for the government to act seriously, to use the period of the six-month hoist for preparing a new budget which will adopt the recommendations of the Auditor General and show Canadians clearly and demonstrably that not only does the government want to cut back spending by a few million dollars, but that it wants to give a considerably higher percentage of the gross national product back to the private sector in order to return incentives for initiative to the people of Canada. They must feel they have their part to play in developing this country. Mr. Speaker, this government governs a ribbon of country 5,000 miles long in which 80 per cent of the population live within 60 miles of the United States border.
November 30, 1976

If ever a country needed to have a less strong centralist government and stronger provincial governments, certainly that country is Canada.
I hope my arguments have convinced hon. members of the foolishness of this bill, of its lack of significance and of the lack of will on the part of the government to do anything concrete with respect to restraint. I hope they will vote in favour of the six-month hoist. If the amendment is adopted, 1 hope the government will do what is necessary to show that it is serious about putting in order the economy and its control over spending.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
1 was pleased to see the government finally admit the necessity for restraint, after many years of no restraint. Therefore, I do not criticize the end the government alleges it wishes to achieve by this bill, but I do question some of the means it is using to obtain it. As a member of parliament from the maritime provinces, I am desperately concerned about the effects of the repeal of section 272 of the Railway Act. That section provides the statutory requirement that railways shall maintain certain rates on export grain and flour from specified points on the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence Seaway ports to maritime ports.
Hon. members have commented on the "at and east" subsidies. The transport committee of the greater Moncton chamber of commerce completed a significant study of the effects of repealing section 272 of the Railway Act. Other hon. members, particularly those from maritime provinces, have already mentioned the effects of such repeal. They are of the utmost importance and I shall list 11 of them this afternoon: first, the increased cost of Canadian flour in foreign markets; second, the loss of foreign markets; third, the loss of foreign currency generated by the flour trade; fourth, the loss of traffic to Canadian ports and Canadian transportation agencies and carriers; fifth, the loss of income to western grain growers; sixth, the loss of employment in the flour milling industry; seventh, the loss of employment in Canadian ports, particularly maritime ports; eighth, the higher railway costs since there will be less traffic to cover overhead; ninth, the loss of employment for Canadian railway workers; tenth, the flour mill at Halifax depends on export markets for a considerable volume of its business. It participates in cargo lots made up by other Canadian mills and exported by Halifax and Saint John. If the Halifax mill must ship its flour back to Montreal or Quebec, it will not be competitive and jobs will be lost in Halifax and Saint John. Eleventh, if the Halifax mill closes, mill feeds produced by the Halifax mill will be unavailable in the maritime area, with an increase in cost affecting the livestock and poultry industries.
Restraint of Government Expenditures
How can a government consciously support the repeal of a section of an act which has such far-reaching consequences to the country as a whole? Is it merely choosing at random the program or bill to be cut or repealed? Is this what other members of the House have been referring to as window-dressing? Certainly, this cannot be the work of responsible legislators, or even of responsible bureaucrats-if there are any.
The Moncton chamber of commerce study which I mentioned earlier recommends that the federal government withdraw that portion of the bill which pertains to section 272 of the Railway Act. I fully agree with their suggestion and strongly urge the government to review their handling of this situation. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang)-and recently I have heard him referred to by some nicknames which I will not repeat today-has attempted to compensate for the government's indiscriminate actions by suggesting that other means of transportation be employed to convey the flour and grain from one point to another. May I remind the hon. minister that although this might increase the trucking business, it will result in massive lay-offs in the railway business.
As the member for Moncton, the hub of the maritimes, the transportation centre, it is not difficult for me to recognize the seriousness of this entire matter. This will cause a devastating situation within the constituency of Moncton and the surrounding area. Even the proposed relocation of the branch of the Department of Supply and Services in my area will not begin to make up for the unemployment which will result from the repeal of section 272 of the Railwayy Act. Surely to goodness the Atlantic provinces are as important as other regions in Canada and should be treated as such! The repeal of section 272 is discriminatory, and the burden will weigh heavily on the entire Atlantic economy. The Atlantic provinces will not stand by and let this be done.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lumley) has stated that those who oppose this bill speak with a forked tongue. I wish to exclude myself from this category: those who make such remarks usually speak with a forked tongue. Although there are some harsh measures in the bill, we must realize that this is a time of economic restraint in this country. If certain programs must be done away with, it is the less important and less necessary ones that should be eliminated. There is little doubt that Opportunities for Youth and agencies known as Information Canada and the Company of Young Canadians fall into this category. They should never have been set up in the first place. That was an irresponsible act of the government, to start with. The repeal of section 272 of the Railway Act is not a feasible solution because of the ill effects of such action.
There are many government departments that could follow much more stringent economic practices. The expensive government project known as "Save 10" which falls under the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, is ample proof of the waste inherent in government offices. There are other many well-publicized government programs which could well benefit from stringent cutbacks. I am thinking specifically of

November 30, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures the bilingualism program and the Anti-Inflation Board and its regulations. The government has spent millions of dollars on its language training program, and now it finally admits that it would have been more beneficial had it been started in the schools. Again, a government in a hurry to get nowhere. Does this mean that they have misallocated their resources? I, for one, find this especially confusing, since I had been proclaiming for years the advantages of implementing this program in the schools, in a national, uniform, integrated, non-separate educational system costing much less.
The Anti-Inflation Board is another excellent example of the government spending millions to save thousands. Certainly this is not good economics or business sense, but it is typical government arithmetic. This demonstrates, most definitely, the lack of management qualities on the part of the government. The member for Restigouche (Mr. Harquail) has accused the provincial government of New Brunswick of spending federal moneys poorly. I cannot dispute this statement and might add that this particular money was probably used to pay for the steering-wheel of a Bricklin. My only hope is that the federal government is not trying to compete with the New Brunswick government to see who can spend most money most frivolously.
Possibly it would help if the government were to take a constructive look at the departments which require a good deal of house-cleaning. For example, let us consider the Department of Manpower and Immigration. I wonder if hon. members on the government side have any idea what happens when a person attempts to apply for employment with the Manpower department. I will give you an example. One unemployed young person entered an Ottawa Canada Manpower office and had practically to force the employee to register him as unemployed. This could be one reason why the employment statistics are only a facade to cloak the distasteful facts which would not show the government in good stead. At this point the constituent consulted another person to see if the Manpower office would inform him if a position was available. The reply, of course, was "not likely", and the applicant would have to return to the office each day to see if any positions were vacant. Approximately one month later the constituent received a form asking whether he was employed. The office of Manpower had provided no assistance to the person, although there were enough employees in the office to go in groups knocking on the doors of employers.
Is this any way to operate an employment agency? Is that restraint? May I remind the government that before one can provide employment, one must destroy the irregularities and inefficiencies of the employment agency. We have another excellent case here of too many people in an office providing too few services. This is not the fault of the employee but of the system; a system for which the government is responsible. In the government of Canada publication, "The Way Ahead: A Framework for Discussion"-which, again, was probably published at great cost to the taxpayer-the government has stated that in formulating their fiscal policies they intend to "seek the advice and views of all Canadians." It is amusing to

note the sincerity of the government in print, but on the floor of the House of Commons they have done nothing but criticize the constructive opinions of those hon. members kind enough to list alternative ideas for the betterment of the country.
It seems that if the government employed a little business sense and the advice of their counterparts in the House, we would have a significantly more efficient civil service and, hence, a more profitable and productive government. For this reason, I feel that the government should take a closer look at the restraint measures inherent in Bill C-19. Since the repeal of section 272 of the Railway Act has received much unfavourable consideration in the House over the past few days, I would suggest that the members on the government side consider amending this proposed legislation, instead of merely employing their majority status to pass legislation which obviously is not to the advantage of Canada as a whole.
This bill on government restraint does not go far enough in cutting out government waste, duplication and inefficiency. It does nothing to increase productivity. It goes too far in repealing section 272 of the Railway Act. If the Minister of Transport would withdraw that particular clause, I sincerely believe the bill might go through smoothly. As things are, it seems he is desirous of having the House continue to waste time. The government should cut down its expenditures and give us honest administration and good government. This is not the way to do it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for giving me the opportunity to speak on Bill C-19. I did not have the opportunity to make any remarks during the debate on the Speech from the Throne, but after I had an opportunity to examine Bill C-19 I thought, "I now have my opportunity."
I have listened carefully to what has been said in the last few days in the discussion pertaining to Bill C-19. It never ceases to amaze me that some of the members who sit across the way are so concerned when we attempt to deal with the problems the government is facing in terms of restraint. One would think they would be happy to hear about the situation as we see it and the solutions which we believe to be necessary. A bill such as the one before us concerns all phases of government-the entire spectrum of government. The only way in which it can be meaningfully discussed is by covering every area in which restraint programs have been or could be introduced. What this bill needs is not a six months' hoist; it needs to be replaced by another bill which might be called, for example, an expenditure control bill.
Looking at this measure, we find it is an act to amend or repeal certain statutes to enable restraint of certain government expenditures. What expenditures? The ones we are primarily concerned about as an opposition have not been mentioned. The government wants to deal with adult occupational training. Well, I think that if they were to scrap the whole bill it would not amount to a saving of much more than "Air Lang" which has cost the Canadian people a great deal
November 30, 1976

of money. The best thing about this bill is the proposal to scrap the Company of Young Canadians. While they were at it, I do not know why the government did not deal similarly with the OFY and LIP programs, too. I have some sympathy with LIP, though. I have suggested on more than one occasion that the government would do me a favour if they took my LIP program and gave it to areas where it was really needed.
Another part of the bill concerns family allowances. I shall have more to say about that in a moment. I can never understand why money is paid under this act to people who really do not need it, and recovered by way of income tax so that it can be redistributed. Then we come to the limitation placed upon industrial development incentives cutting out applications as of December 1, 1976. I really do not know whether in the end this will result in meaningful savings. The legislation setting up Information Canada is to be repealed. Why this organization was set up in the first place is beyond me. I do not know what was wrong with the earlier set-up under Statistics Canada. Other clauses in the bill have to do with the western grains stabilization act. Then there is a proposal to repeal section 272 of the Railway Act. This, as one hon. member has pointed out, will serve to benefit Montreal at the expense of the Maritimes.
What is the bill likely to achieve in terms of restraint? The best way for the government to achieve its target and stay within its guidelines is seriously to consider appointing a comptroller of the treasury, someone who would approve expenditures, someone who would give final approval to expenditures prepared for payment by the respective departments and take responsibility for them. In certain respects, cutbacks in departmental expenditure, though a long-established practice, discriminate unfairly against taxpayers in certain regions. For instance, this year's budgetary restraints imposed upon the Post Office Department can hardly be termed reasonable in light of recent increases in postal rates. In any case, they have serious consequences to people at the constituency level.
This is why restraints or cutbacks are unfair to certain groups of taxpayers. In any city, new housing developments are under way. Construction is commenced at different times, so completion time-frames will vary. As a rule, approval is granted for the development of projects adjacent to areas which are already developed. As these are started, further development permits are granted affecting new areas which are adjacent to areas already developed or to areas in the advanced development stage.

DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REQUIRE DEPARTMENT TO REPORT TO PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
that Bill C-201, an Act to amend the Department of Justice Act (annual report), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak once more on Bill C-201. Since a copy of the bill was made available to hon. members and I have been putting forward this legislation during a number of legislatures, I sincerely hope it will meet with unanimous support in this House. It does not aim at a parliamentary revolution, but simply proposes to solve an anomaly within the federal government.
To explain the matter briefly, the federal Department of Justice is the only federal department that does not table its yearly activity report in this House. For this reason, Parliament has no control on the operations and financial administration of the department. Of course the department's estimates are referred to the standing committee as any other department's. But as I said, it is the only department that does not table an annual report. Therefore, as stated in the explanatory notes:

The Department of Justice is the only department which does not submit a report to Parliament. The purpose of this amendment is to correct this anomaly, to insure a better parliamentary control of the Department...
-by members of this House, and above alland to improve its efficiency.

November 30, 1976
Department of Justice Act
Mr. Speaker, the amendment reads in part:
... on or before the 30th of September next following, or, if Parliament is not then sitting, on any first five days next thereafter that Parliament is sitting, submit to Parliament a report showing the operations of the Department of Justice for that fiscal year."
To me, it is not so much the date suggested in the said clause which is important, but rather the rule requiring that the department should file his annual report as the others do.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if for administrative reasons, the date above were enough to entail disregard of the rule and thus break the unanimity of hon. members, I would accept an amendment to the bill to make it acceptable to all members of the House since the main thing is to enable hon. members to get acquainted with the internal administration of that most important department.
1 have nothing more to add, Mr. Speaker, because I would like some of my colleagues to voice their views and more especially to have that important bill passed today.

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the leader of the Social Credit Party, the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin), for bringing in this bill. I feel there should be a report from the Department of Justice, as one who has been actively engaged in matters affecting the administration of justice for a number of years in this House. It is one of the most important departments of government. Without the administration of justice and the proper administration of justice, without the real freedom that flows from the rule of law which is the very basis of our parliamentary and democratic process, everything else, of course, fails.
I am interested in this bill and I give it my whole support. I am not going to talk for too long, but I want to mention a few of my concerns about why there should be a report. There has, of late, been a very serious situation in the administration of justice across the country with reference to the various attorneys general's departments of the provinces. I refer to the question of privacy.
Last session we were severely criticized for opposing Bill C-83. If Bill C-83 had gone through, it would have allowed electronic devices to wiretap people's telephones all across the country so as to enable others to listen in on private conversations, receive private information, industrial, corporate and individual data and private conversations generally. No doubt, as we have seen in the famous case under the Nixon administration in the United States, wiretapping would even enter the political arena.
Bill C-83 removed the necessity for giving notice to an individual whose telephone was to be wiretapped by an electronic device. I opposed that removal, not only on second reading but strenuously in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. The best we could squeeze out of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) and the former solicitor general was that notice would have to be given within a period

of five years. Well, Mr. Speaker, Five years is a long time and most people whose telephones were being wiretapped would have left the country, or at least left the community and moved on somewhere else.
I contend that the provision in the Criminal Code that notice must be given within 90 days must remain in the Code. Both I and my party are in favour of providing that an extension at this time could easily be sanctioned by a judge if the necessity arose, for example when investigating syndicated crime. Secondly, there has been a long-established principle in the administration of justice that in order to protect the liberty of the individual a conversation between a person and his solicitor or counsel is privileged and confidential. Even a conversation between a patient and a doctor is not privileged in court, whereas a conversation between a solicitor and his client is confidential.
The reason for this practice, which has grown up in our common law over many centuries, is that the individual must be protected against the all-powerful state. But what has been taking place in this country, not only in the province of Ontario but in other provinces? Even the province of Alberta is now wiretapping conversations between lawyers and their clients. One might almost suggest that now we will have to remove telephones from law offices.
I have had one example of this brought to my attention, Mr. Speaker. I have no proof that it has happened, but I have certainly had letters to this effect. I agree it is an extreme case, but it does deal with the question of privacy. If a lawyer visits a client while he is incarcerated, having been charged with the commission of a crime that calls for him to remain in jail, the little rooms where you interview your client have been electronically wiretapped. This is an erosion of the fundamental principle of privacy and a breach of the most fundamental principle of civil rights.
A third matter that I think might bear some reporting is this: there has been a long-standing principle that anyone charged with an offence, no matter how heinous the offence may be, has the right to remain silent. Not too many people realize that this principle exists. When a person charged with an offence is on trial before a judge and jury, or before a judge without a jury, he need say nothing. The onus is on the Crown to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. When I use the term "beyond reasonable doubt", I mean the kind of doubt that any reasonable man might have in his business affairs, or in dealing with his family matters, or that a woman might have when dealing with her family or business matters.
A practice is now developing across the country whereby the police are able to do what the courts cannot do. A judge cannot ask a prisoner in the dock, "Were you there? Tell me what happened". The rules relating to voluntary statements are being usurped. I cannot go into the details because there is a case right on this point, but in some types of murder there may be a question of the prisoner's insanity and he is sent to a mental hospital to undergo psychiatric treatment by psychiatrists and psychologists and other scientific and technical personnel skilled in medical and psychological experimenta-
November 30, 1976

tion. That information is then given to the police or to the Crown. Surely an interview by a psychiatrist who asks questions about the background of an individual, his childhood environment, his problems at school and with his parents, perhaps a division in the home, problems in the community, business arrangements and reaction to certain circumstances, could not be admitted unless it was given voluntarily as a statement to the police. This is an attempt to get in the back door what cannot be got in the front door.
I know of a case involving an individual confined to a mental hospital following the most serious charge of murder. He was taken out of the mental hospital for a remand in court some five hours before he was needed. He was interrogated for at least 2Vi hours. How could such a statement be voluntary? The fundamental rules of jurisprudence which we follow establish as a test whether the statement is true or false, and how could you decide that when it was made by a person confined to a mental institution? If that does not cause frustration among defence lawyers across this country, and does not represent an erosion of civil rights, then there is no frustration and no erosion of any kind.
I could continue to talk on this matter for quite some time, but I do not wish to delay this measure. It is an excellent bill and it will receive my support. These matters should be reported to parliament, because in this way the representatives of the people of Canada would have this information which too often is denied by the executives of governments today.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I rise to speak on the matter presently before this House, may I first take this opportunity to congratulate the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin) on his recent election as leader of the Social Credit Party. If the hon. member is able to lead with the same wisdom and insight as his predecessor did, Canada will be well served.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As this House already knows, Bill C-201 as proposed by the hon. member for Lotbiniere would amend the Department of Justice Act, Revised Statutes of Canada 1970, chapter J-2, to provide that the Minister of Justice shall submit an annual report to parliament on the operations of the department. The report would be submitted after the termination of each fiscal year, or on or before September 30 next following or, if parliament is not then sitting, on any first five days next thereafter that parliament is sitting.
The Department of Justice has not been required to submit an annual report in the past because its primary responsibility or function has been to provide legal services to other departments and agencies of the government. There has existed, and still exists, a solicitor-client relationship between the Department of Justice and the other departments and agencies it represents. However, in recent years the department has expanded its role by becoming involved in new programs
Department of Justice Act
relating to legal research and law reform and other programs such as cost-sharing of legal aid services in Canada.
In view of these new activities, it is perhaps time that an annual report such as proposed by the hon. member should be considered. A report of this nature might provide the public with more and better information than is now available concerning the activities of the department. Members of this House may be interested to know that the departmental counterpart in the United States submits an annual report which is very informative and interesting.
There is one minor objection we have to the bill, and it is that the bill does not provide for a sufficient period within which to file the annual report. In this regard it should be noted that chapter 24, R.S.C. 1970, provides that the Minister of Communications has until January 31 next following the end of any fiscal year within which he or she shall submit an annual report on the operations of the Department of Communications. Similar statutory provisions exist in respect of other departments such as the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. In recent years this date has been found to be more practical or useful in terms of available information and the ability of the departments to produce it.
In view of the foregoing, Mr. Speaker, we have no objection to the bill, provided that it is amended so as to delete the phrase "30th of September" and substitutes therefor "31st day of January". I am pleased to learn that the mover of this bill is agreeable to the proposed amendment.
The Minister of Justice, the Department of Justice and the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice welcome this opportunity to continue with our long-established policy of responsiveness and openness in our ongoing efforts to ensure justice for all Canadians. This private member's bill gives us the opportunity to display, once again, our flexibility; to show, through action, that the Minister of Justice is both receptive to and appreciative of ideas from members of the House of Commons without regard to where they may sit in this chamber.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Andras that Bill C-19, to amend or repeal certain statutes to enable restraint of government expenditures, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Holmes (p. 1393).
