subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at five o'clock I was talking about the voluntary restraints that were implemented by the Post Office Department and what I thought was the unreasonable position in which that placed many people in this country. I was talking about developments in the cities and what happens when there is a restraint program arbitrarily agreed to within a department which affects areas where development takes place after the imposition of the controls.
The point I was trying to make was that the injury resulted when one project or one district had been completed and mail delivery service had been instituted in that area, but because of the imposition of a restraint program a few months or a few weeks later, an adjacent area which had taken longer to develop and become a fully residential area was denied the same service simply because it was caught in the middle of the program. This kind of program is unfair and unwarranted. A cut-back in any department should be of such a nature that it does not discriminate, and it must have the same impact on all.
In the last decade even though the Post Office Department has experienced a 50 per cent increase in staff and a 50 per cent increase in the cost of operation, together with a recent increase in the price of postage, it is strange that the service has deteriorated to an intolerable level. There is no question in my mind that some form of action on the part of the government is long overdue.

Bill C-19 is an attempt to plug a leak in the dike. I want to talk for a few minutes about the Company of Young Canadians that was brought into being by the late Lester B. Pearson. The tale is told in a book entitled "The Big Rip-off," written by a lady by the name of Erna Koffman. It clearly illustrates the fumbling, bumbling, mismanagement, deceit, and distortion which took place not only within the confines of the political offices responsible for the program but also within the sanctions of the public servants responsible for its administration. In retrospect one would think that the players in this CYC game outside the realm of politics were selected on the basis of their incompetence to perform within the intent of the legislation, with unexcelled competence to milk the system.
No one was more pleased than I to see the Company of Young Canadians go down the pipe, regrettably too late, after the program had cost the people of Canada millions of dollars. What did Erna Koffman say about the program and some of its activities? How did the program work? For the record I should like to read one paragraph from the book "The Big Rip-off' which I think deals very clearly with how responsible were the administrators of that program. This is what she had to say:
Theoretically, any community in Canada that wanted to embark on a self-help programme could request the services of a 'volunteer' of the CYC. However, since shortly after its inception, the CYC has run into flak, and criticism has poured into Ottawa from many parts of the country where the CYC has been operating, accusing the Company of stirring up trouble or encouraging troublesome elements in Communities. The Premier of one Western Province ordered the Company out of his province. It seems that wherever there are civic disturbances, CYC workers seem to be around.
We talk about restraint, yet this government put millions of dollars into a program which was responsible for this kind of activity.
I wonder if the government still thinks that a comptroller general, a chief financial officer, could not have prevented this kind of waste of public funds relative to this program. Does the government not now feel that this most significant recommendation of the Auditor General should be acted upon immediately, pending findings of the commission set up to investigate government spending? We do not need a royal commission to tell us that a program is wrong in principle, that it is mismanaged and far too expensive. According to Bill C-19, the CYC program would now be cancelled as part of the restraint program. That is like locking the barn door after the horse has been stolen.
What did the program achieve? It served to inform the taxpayers of this country that, in the face of growing unemployment, stop-gap programs were not the answer. It served to inform the Canadian public that a sound economic policy was lacking. The program told us that stop-gap programs were not workable when-in the absence of sound economic policy and good sense taxes were rising, welfare programs were strained and the cost of living was rising-the government poured millions of dollars into programs which only aggravated the unemployment situation. What we expected to see in Bill C-19 was not the cancellation of a program which should never have
November 30, 1976

begun, but positive steps to demonstrate to this House that the government is serious in its announced desire to curtail spending, and particularly irresponsible spending.
Every member of this House is concerned about the statement made by the Auditor General that he fears parliament and, indeed, the government have lost control over spending. What has been a matter of concern to members of parliament for a number of years has been forcibly brought to the fore by none other than the man who audits government accounts. Committee recommendations and pleas by members of parliament have been ignored, and I ask if the government is now going to ignore the warnings of J. J. Macdonell.
What did Mr. Macdonell say in his warning to the government? I wish to quote from an article written by Michael Van Dusen of the Financial Times services and printed in the Edmonton Journal of November 23. It is an article entitled "Crown Corporations Spend Without Control". I will only put a paragraph of this on the record. This is what Mr. Van Dusen said:
Underlining the inadequacy of the controls the federal government budgetary expenditures were $34 billion in 1976 but only 34 man-years were devoted to financial administration policy and evaluation-about one man year per billion dollars.
Is this a proper ratio by which to effect controls? I suggest it is not.
What are some examples of what the Auditor General was talking about? Mr. Van Dusen talks about $4 million and other considerations valued at $702,000 plus an annual rent of $241,000, paid by the Department of the Environment for 55 acres of waterfront property in Vancouver. The property was rented by the former tenant for $48,180 per year. It was from this tenant that the government had originally acquired the leasehold.
The second point about which the Auditor General is concerned, and which is dealt with in this article, is the $828,000 which was spent by the Canadian International Development Agency for the purchase and modification of a boat which was destined never to sail, and a fivefold over-expenditure of $559,000 by the Public Service Commission staff training and development fund for which the commission asked a compensating appropriation of $747,000 in the next budget year, $200,000 more than they really needed.
I want for a moment to talk about government office space waste which is equal to 139 football fields. I am referring to an article written by Don Sellar which was printed in the Edmonton Journal, and my constituents are very much concerned. This article refers to the Auditor General and says:
Applying the government's own guildelines for office requirements, he concluded that the bureaucracy occupies more than 30 per cent more space than it ought to.
What the auditor-general doesn't say in his annual repdrt, tabled Monday in Parliament, is that this situation is likely to worsen in the years ahead.
I can understand why this cabinet occupies 30 per cent more office space than it needs. This cabinet is fat and complacent and not willing to govern. I can understand why it occupies more space, but why does the bureaucracy occupy more space
Restraint of Government Expenditures than necessary? The Auditor General pressed for information with respect to these leases and with respect to the projected requirements of this excess space, and that information was denied. Mr. Sellar went on as follows:
After looking into the process by which eight federal departments and two agencies determine their additional space requirements, he finds there is an "absence of sufficient documentation to justify requests for space."
Even worse, there is no procedure whereby the Department of Public Works can reclaim surplus offices for reallocation to other departments or agencies.
The way the government accommodation game is played, it seems that once a department manages to wangle some office space, there is virtually no way DPW can get it back, even if the rooms are vacant or "under-utilized."
I simply ask, who in government has the responsibility in this regard? The article goes on:
"In 13 cases... documentation was insufficient for our purposes or was unavailable," the auditor-general says, more in sorrow than in anger. "In the other five, examination of the reported figures revealed that space use exceeded the relevant guidelines by more than 30 per cent in three cases."
One departmental horror story uncovered by the special inquiry occurred 15 months ago when an organizational unit moved into 103,000 square feet of new office space, including 18,000 square feet reserved for two new activities which should be getting under way now.
They may not get under way in the next 18 months. I do not need to bring to the attention of the House any more of the warnings of the Auditor General to parliament or what the Auditor General wants us to do, but I am saying that there are people in the cabinet who must be responsible for this phase of government, and it is incumbent upon them to act.
With regard to the Family Allowances Act which is dealt with in Bill C-19, for years some of us in this House have advocated the removal of the universal aspect of this legislation. Many millions of dollars could be saved simply by changing the fund so that it pays only on application. The family allowance serves a useful purpose, but its usefulness becomes questionable when universality is applied. Rather than take the course the government has taken, namely, to freeze at the 1975 level the rates at which amounts are paid to residents of provinces specifying rates for family allowance, the universal aspect should be reviewed immediately.
The government could also save money on administrative costs by not pushing out cheques to people who do not want or do not need them, and if the Income Tax Department refused to take back money that was paid to taxpayers by way of family allowance only to redistribute it again in the next year. The government should act as quickly as possible to set the upper limits of qualification for family allowance by statute, and forget the freeze. It seems to me that would be a more equitable distribution of the taxpayer's dollar.
Information Canada has been scrapped. I do not know what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) intended when he put this little entity together. What was wrong with the Dominion Bureau of Statistics-except the name "Dominion"? All I can say is that Information Canada is good for the government if the government is good, but it is bad for the government if the government is bad. I suggest to you that is why Information Canada is now something in the past.

Let me make it clear that within an acceptable time frame certain positions in the civil service could have been declared bilingual and then filled by way of promotion. Then it would not have been necessary to immerse senior civil servants at 55, 56 or 57 years of age.

A program designed to educate the children of Canada in both official languages-French in the rest of Canada and English in Quebec-commencing at grade 1, would have allowed an orderly transition from primarily a country with two official languages but separated by regions, those regions not being able to communicate with each other in the language of their choice. In a decade or two the problem would have looked after itself simply by implementing the education of children in the other language at the grade school level. In the context of a restraint program all of this would have had a noticeable effect in the intervening years.
A federal-provincial conference could have been held to determine on what basis the provincial governments wanted to approach the program. I suggest a per capita grant could have been offered by the federal government to every province that wanted to participate. Would this not have been the better solution in 1969 than to go on to a crash program and try to immerse 55 year old civil servants in a French program, and then retire them two weeks after they graduate? I will say no more about this program, Mr. Speaker, except that some of us who advocated this as far back as the day it was thought of are now vindicated because in the Speech from the Throne the government announced this course of action.

speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, I was just leading into that because I thought that little anecdote, which comes from the annals of the Liberal party, was a pretty good introduction to the title of this bill, because the days when they had horses on the payroll in Petawawa have their counterpart in the way the government operates today. Today we are debating Bill C-19, "An Act to Amend or Repeal Certain Statutes to Enable Restraint of Government Expenditures." It is a very welcome title-it almost makes your heart skip a beat. One is encouraged because one believes that finally the government is serious about restraint. But then you read through the bill and your encouragement changes to discouragement. You realize that the bill is another example of a public relations job and that the government is not talking about restraint, it is talking about petty cash. It spills more than it is trying to save in this bill.
I do not think we ever want to turn down an opportunity to save the taxpayers' money, but this bill is rather like a leper going to a clinic saying, "I do not want the cure. All I want is something to cover the gangrene."
I should like to deal with just three of the aspects of this bill and draw the attention of hon. members to what I think is a piece of sham which the government is perpetrating on members of the House, and certainly trying to perpetrate on members of the public. When we turn to clause 3 of the bill we find that under this clause the Company of Young Canadians shall be deemed to have ceased to exist on April 1. Then I look at the budget of the Company of Young Canadians and I find that in 1973-74 its expenditures amounted to $2.8 million, and in 1974-75 to $3,722 million. The forecast for 1975-76 is $5.5 million. As I have mentioned, the Company of Young Canadians was deemed to have ceased to exist on April 1, 1976. Then I turn to the Auditor General's report at page 24, where I find that, immediately before the dissolution of the company, severance payments totalling $185,500 were made to volunteer members. Whoever heard of volunteer members getting severance pay?
I thought that if you volunteered to work for an organization, you were a volunteer. Yet we have the ludicrous situation of people supposedly being so caught up with the ideal that the government presented to them in the Company of Young
November 30, 1976

Canadians that they volunteer their services to the Canadian people for the betterment of Canada, and now they are being given severance pay. As a cute addendum to that I notice that the government did not even have the authority to make that kind of severance pay to the CYC. That is the kind of thing we are facing in this bill. We are dealing with something that no longer exists. We are dealing with one of the smallest budget appropriations that we have in the budget estimates, and we are dealing with the case of the government taking upon itself an authorization to which it had no right.
Meanwhile, back at the ranch, we have Quick Draw McGraw and Baba Louie. To represent those characters you can pick any two of the ministers in the front row. For convenience's sake we can take the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), and his sidekick, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald). Here we have a discussion of $5 million to be saved by the dissolution of the Company of Young Canadians, while these two gentlemen are saying, "What do you know, we would like to sell some atomic reactors to foreign countries. Let us look around for good salesmen. What is their commission? We won't bother about that. We will come to that two years later when people start asking questions. But if the commission comes to $20 million, as it has now, what is the difference? It is only $20 million".
Then we have the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) casuistry today when in effect he said, "Sure, the former auditor general wrote to me three and a half years ago and I passed the letter on to the then president of the treasury board. I asked him to look into it, but I heard no more, so what could I do about it? I mean, my hands were tied because they did not answer my note." Maybe that is a good indication of why the country is in trouble. We are faced today with the effrontery of the Prime Minister telling us that, since he heard no more with regard to the memo, he is no longer responsible. I would like to refer to the letter of March 27, 1973. Notice the casual tone that the Prime Minister used when he discussed this with the then president of the treasury board and said:
... I wonder if the best course might not be for you to organize a discussion of the question with Messrs. Turner, Goyer and Sharp.
He organizes a discussion about $20 million. Mr. Speaker, that was no time to organize a discussion. What we needed was an investigation, and three and a half years later the Prime Minister has the effrontery to say in the House that he tried but it did not work, that since it was a Crown corporation he cannot be held responsible for the $20 million. Today we are debating a $5 million appropriation to the Company of Young Canadians. It is just a sleight of hand trick. Get their attention, listen to what they are saying, but meanwhile watch closely what they are doing.
One of the clauses in the bill deals with the disbanding of Information Canada. I do not mind Information Canada being disbanded. Nobody will complain about that. It means the saving of another $10 million expropriation for an organization whose responsibility it was to make the government look good.
Restraint of Government Expenditures Now, as the hon. member for Edmonton East has said, it has outlived its usefulness and can be disbanded. This makes it look as though the government is really interested in saving public funds.
I turn now to another aspect of the bill and it concerns personnel rather than budgetary considerations. I have mentioned before in this House an occasion when, together with other members of the special parliamentary committee, I was moving across Canada to listen to what the Canadian people has to say on the subject of immigration. We came to Edmonton and, as was the case in so many cities, there were demonstrations against these so-called Fascist perpetrators who had come from the House of Commons and were talking about that racist green paper. The special feature of the demonstrations in Edmonton was the fact that the demonstrators were Maoists. Their signs said they were Maoists. They had a bulletin which they shared with anyone who cared to read it in which they advised that their next meeting would be held in the office of the Company of Young Canadians in Edmonton.
The saving of millions of dollars by disbanding the Company of Young Canadians is one thing. We are always glad to save public money. But for all those years it attracted people who were not interested in the welfare of Canada as we had known it. They were interested in using the finances and the mechanism of government to tear down Canada and its institutions. They were being funded by the government to bring about, to the extent they were able, the demise of Canada. This is another reason-and it is even more important than financial considerations-why the Company of Young Canadians should be disbanded.
To a lesser degree, the same is true of Information Canada. I am not by any means suggesting that Information Canada was a hotbed of revolutionaries or Maoists. But 1 am saying it was a superfluous organization. We have done without it for six months now, and I have not noticed that anybody has missed it. So there has been an appropriation of $10 million every year for very little purpose.
I suppose the government had the idea, when it was formed, that there would no longer be any necessity to maintain individual information centres within the departments, and so on. But what really happened? We found that each of the ministries still maintained its own publications office.
We ran into the same thing today when discussing the budget of the National Film Board whose branches include an agency for the processing and development of films for all the departments within the government. The budget runs to something like $1.3 million and it is supposed to service all the agencies of the federal government in Ottawa. One of the problems is that the government agencies in Ottawa are not using these services. They are still developing their own films, producing their own pictures, doing their own PR work, even though the Film Board has evidently-and we take their word for it-one of the finest labs in the country.
The same thing happened in the case of Information Canada, so I believe it is a good thing that the government has finally seen fit to disband that organization. Nevertheless, we

November 30, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures must look carefully at what is going on elsewhere. This represents a $10 million cut, but consider what is happening at Statistics Canada. One could go on to recite the endless litany of inequities there. One such case came to notice in the Ottawa Citizen of November 4. A respected columnist, a former member of this House, wrote:
With thousands of Canadian graduates unemployed or under-employed, the wife was given educational leave worth $13,000 to complete her BA. Chretien might be curious about why the wife was given her position at the agency if she didn't have the educational qualifications or why she was given a freebee to complete her education if her qualifications were considered adequate to hire her.
A lot of questions have to be answered about the hiring policies of Statistics Canada. I wonder how many millions of dollars are involved there.
We have often heard Mirabel mentioned in the course of this debate. We might adopt an American revolutionary slogan and talk about millions for Mirabel but not one cent for the farmers on whose land it was built. I recall that a year and a half ago there was a demonstration of farmers on the Hill. They burned bales of hay. These farmers owned the land upon which Mirabel was built. The land had been expropriated seven years ago but it had still not been paid for. Their property was taken away to make room for a multi-million dollar structure which is still partly vacant. We realize now that we never really needed it. We talk about saving $10 million on Information Canada. How many millions are involved in Mirabel? Four hundred million dollars?
The we move on to another chorus in the litany-Campeau Corporation. The Canadian people will be asked to pay an extra $300 million because of a deal the government arranged with regard to a long term lease which could have been obtained much more cheaply had it been done in another way. And so it goes on. While we talk about restraint in one area of government we waste money by the bucketful in others.
I should like to move on to clause 10, the clause which deals with industrial research and development. The act is to be amended to allow researchers to finish current projects. That is commendable. There are many good projects which would have otherwise been completely wasted. The legislation will eventually bring about the cessation of all research under this program. Being just a farm boy, I must say that a measure of this kind reminds me of a farmer who had a cow which milked very well but which ate voraciously. The farmer did not want to pay for the food the cow was consuming so gradually, day by day, he gave it less and less. "Finally," he said, "you know I almost had that critter to the point at which it did not eat at all, and then the crazy thing died on me."
On one hand the government talks about increasing productivity, increasing the gross national product. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) is encouraging the unions to increase productivity. On the other hand the government is saying: no more research under our auspices.
I remember just about a year ago one of the members from eastern Ontario arranging for a group of members to take a tour of the National Research Council facilities in Ottawa.
This was a good gesture on his part and it certainly was a good experience for us. We could see exactly what the government was investing in research. It was an interesting trip. As we got off the bus, what did we find? There were about 50 or a hundred scientists walking around in hard hats picketing members of parliament because their research funds had been cut off.
Historically, Mr. Speaker, research scientists have not been picketers. We may not always agree with their projects, but believe me these scientists are not at home on the picket line. They are at home with a test tube, a Bunsen burner, a microscope, and all kinds of laboratory equipment. Theirs is the quiet world of the laboratory, not the picket line. But they were desperate. They saw years of experiments were going to go down the tube. They saw all their investment, ingenuity, creativity and time would now be wasted because the government was cutting off their funds.
It strikes me that Canada of all countries already has a record of being one of the most niggardly in the area of industrial research. I note that Mr. John Shepherd, executive director of the Science Council of Canada, has had this to say:
The spectacle of R & D budgets being cut, basic research being eroded, and federal stimulant programs under painful review has worked to make the climate for industrial innovation decidedly bleak.
Then I think hon. members will be interested in this comment:
However, Canada's performance in transforming ideas into products ranked with Portugal in a 1972 study. Canada and Portugal were the two countries in the western world where industry spends the least on industrial R & D as a percentage of total R & D spending.
Industry in Canada is not a good spender on research and I think needs to be jacked up in that regard. Nevertheless, the government has to complement what industry does. Right now it is doing this; industry is doing almost nothing and the government is doing almost nothing. But my point is that although industry is doing nothing, the government ought to be doing something.
It is also well known that multinationals in Canada are not continuing to do research. Why should they, Mr. Speaker? They do most of their research at their home base, which I think is not the way it ought to be. The government continually says that we should make our companies more Canadian, that we should Canadianize our industry.
Just yesterday the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) announced quotas for the textile industry because he wants to protect Canadian industry. How in the world can we Canadianize our industry if we cut off all research to Canadian industry? How will our research scientists live if the world of ideas is cut off from them? I think Mr. Shepherd put it very well when he said that Canada's performance in transforming ideas into products ranked with Portugal in a 1972 study. Transforming ideas into products is what research is all about. Yet government wants to cut off research funds, which I think is almost unforgivable.

November 30, 1976

Actually, Mr. Speaker, industry fares very well. Under this bill a researcher is at least allowed to finish his project. He can apply for a grant, sufficient not to waste his project. But with medical research there is not even the day of grace by which they must finish their projects. Certainly the Medical Research Council has not done as well as industry. 1 know a research scientist in Vancouver, Dr. Tze, who is doing research in diabetics, something that Canada is known around the world for pioneering. A year ago he was half way through a research project involving rats. Then the announcement came that his grants were going to be cut off, which meant that not only was his year's work done but that two or three years' work was done. The control group had no problem but the experimental group was killed off half way through the project. In order to start up again he would have to get another set and begin all over once more.
It so happened, Mr. Speaker, that someone got wind of this tragedy-perhaps I should call it travesty-and brought it to the attention of a television hotliner in Vancouver who had him on his show. After hearing his story he then said, "Well, what do you folks think? Do you think this ought to happen?" Then the lines were opened and the money came in to the tune of $26,000 so that he could finish his project.
The government is saying that private groups and charitable organizations should take up the slack and kick into the kitty so that research can be carried on. We have a heart fund, a fund for cystic fibrosis, and a fund for rheumatism. But as someone put it to me today, we do not have an organization for every organ of the body; you just cannot collect money this way. I am all in favour of having charitable donations to enable research to be carried on. Indeed, I think the cancer society ought to be commended for the work it is doing. But it cannot do all the work; surely the government has some responsibility in this area.
The government says that private agencies ought to help, and I agree. But in saying that, the government ought also to be consistent. I do not see the government saying that in terms of the economy. We do not see the government saying that private agencies ought to carry all the segments of the economy. No, Mr. Speaker, its arguments point the other way. The government wants to get involved and to mess around in the free enterprise system. I do not hear the government saying we should let more private enterprise become involved in Petro-Can or Syncrude; quite the opposite. If the government wants to encourage more private interest in medical research, at the same time it should also encourage private interest in the economy. All we are saying is that the government should be consistent.
The shameful aspect of all this, Mr. Speaker, is that even up to two years ago the United States was investing six times as much as Canada in medical research. What is the implication of this? It simply means that we face the awful prospect of riding piggyback on the good will of the Americans who are so often castigated by members of this government. So often members talk of the ugly Americans, but by George we sure want to ride them when it comes to taking advantage of their
Restraint of Government Expenditures medical research. We do not turn down their Salk vaccine; that is mighty welcome. I notice we do not mind importing their swine flu vaccine; that is also welcome. We let the Americans do all the research; we just take advantage of it.
Certain kinds of research have implications for industry. There are some pharmaceutical companies which carry on their own research because ultimately it has implications for their industry. After all, if their own researchers make a new discovery or develop a new medicine, the companies will produce that medicine and this will provide dividends.
There are other kinds of research that do not have these kinds of industrial implications. I have in mind medical research that will bring about new techniques in brain surgery, for example, or as has been the case in Canada where Canadians have contributed significantly to the development of better pacers and better techniques for implanting them and for implanting arteries in the heart. This is a significant contribution on the part of Canadian medical research, but that is not the kind of research that produces results for industry. This simply produces benefits for those who suffer from these diseases. There is no industry in the world that is going to contribute to that kind of research. On the contrary, it depends on the good will of the government to help in those areas where there are no industrial benefits, simply human benefits.
A series of cutbacks in medical research has one final implication I should like to point out, and that is in respect of medical training facilities. Hon. members of the House will acknowledge the fact that a good medical training staff in a university is totally dependent upon a good research facility in that university. We cannot simply have a professor of medicine in a medical school reciting like a tape recorder the information he has gleaned from textbooks year after year. A good medical instructor is one who is also active in the lab keeping current with medical research. He is involved in the world of ideas, asking questions, not simply repeating information. This is the kind of atmosphere in which good instructors and professors as well as doctors are produced.
One must ask what is going to happen to the quality of medicine in our country if we continue over the year with the kind of pattern the government is establishing at this time. What will be the quality of medicine in our country if our doctors have to go abroad to get up-to-date and adequate medical training? One might ask how many of the competent and world renowned research scientists, some who have received the Nobel peace prize, are no longer here in Canada because Canada was too niggardly and profligate in other areas to contribute in the field of medical research?
I suggest we will come to the day when we will curse ourselves for allowing the government to waste millions upon millions of dollars in areas that bear no fruit, while at the same time cutting back on grants that would provide us with a better standard of living and a more healthy Canadian population.

November 30, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures
These are the things I feel are shameful about the bill, obviously not the fact that we are going to save money. That is something in respect of which I pay tribute to the government. The fact is we must come back to that old question, "what are these among so many"? Millions of dollars could be saved, yet we are talking about petty cash or the amount the government spills in its negligence.
I trust the government will take another look at this matter, and it is for that reason I support the amendment that there be a six months hoist. Perhaps in this way we can shake up the government so that it will re-evaluate its priorities and realize it is ignoring the most important things in life.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES RESTRAINT ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it may be just coincidence that we are dealing with a bill to amend or repeal certain statutes to enable restraint of government expenditures at a time when newspapers from one end of this country to the other are carrying headlines to the effect that government spending is out of control.
It is common knowledge in this country that we have one standard for the government and another standard for the citizens. We see ministers abusing the trust placed in them, we hear talk about kickbacks and shady deals, and suggestions that the government is guilty of sins of omission or commission. I am reminded that there was a company by the name of Lockheed which was never really guilty of any offence, but a lot of people went to jail because of what that company did.
We are dealing here with another so-called omnibus bill. It deals with adult occupational training, the Company of Young Canadians, the Family Allowances Act, industrial research, Information Canada, the Western Grain Stabilization Act, and the Railway Act. It is difficult to find and deal with one principle in this collection.
Having regard to the Railway Act, the bill simply states that Section 272 of the Railway Act is repealed. We may not be dealing with a large amount of money, but in this short sentence we are dealing with a very large principle. In fact we are breaking an agreement that has lasted for 109 years. Surely if this is what we are intending to do it should be dealt with by a specific statute. If the government can get away with this then it is sure that it would be just as simple to change, amend, or destroy the Crowsnest Pass rates we have in western Canada under the Railway Act. To lump these railway proposals with the Company of Young Canadians takes some nerve and cynicism.
The term "at and east" has been used a great deal during the debate on Bill C-19, but I doubt if there are many hon. members who understand the background of this term. For years Canadian grain and flour were moved through the United States city of Buffalo east to tidewater for export. This naturally caused great concern to the Canadian grain trade and our maritime ports.
In 1960 the Canadian railroads were asked to set up rates that would be competitive with United States rail rates through Buffalo and east to tidewater. This meant that for all points from Georgian Bay on Lake Huron the railway rate was

to be competitive with the United States rail rate prevailing at Buffalo and east. The "at" refers to "at Buffalo." Canadian grain used to move from Buffalo through the Erie Canal out to export positions from there. The Canadian National Railways even had an elevator at Portland, Maine.
If the government can take away this protection under the Railway Act it could do the same thing in western Canada in respect of Crowsnest Pass rates. If it did the same thing the situation would probably be that western Canadian grain would move on U.S. rails to export and we would find ourselves in the same situation on the west coast of Canada as the Atlantic ports found themselves in before Section 272 of the Railway Act was effected. That is why we are taking such a stand on this particular section.
Bill C-19 has much to do with agriculture. At my meetings with various producer groups across this country several concerns have come through from all quarters. First there is the feeling that Canadian agriculture is being downgraded and traded off in international bargaining for industry. The second point is that the influence of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has also been downgraded and he does not have the support of his Cabinet colleagues any longer.
The third great concern is that the government is not committed to supporting a viable Canadian agriculture and that food brokers will be allowed to pick up agricultural products anywhere in the world where they are cheapest. I can give as examples, cheese, tomatoes, mushrooms, beef, tender fruits and so on. If it is to be the decision of the government that the great retail stores are to feed Canadians, and if we follow this to its logical conclusion, then in Canada we will become a nation of agricultural consumers with no produce to sell and eventually no money to buy so-called cheap produce from overseas. We must make a decision concerning whether or not we want Loblaws, Safeway, and other chains to feed Canadians, or whether we want the Canadian farmers to do that job.
Then we have the matter of cheese imports into this country to the extent of 100 million pounds. Surely the Canadian Dairy Commission should be the first receiver rather than the brokers. We can produce 90 per cent of the specialty cheese in Canada. We have the importation of Taiwan tomatoes when Canada does not even recognize Taiwan. We have no trading agreements with that country.
Clause 15 of this bill, which would repeal the so-called "at and east" rates will directly effect the export of western grain and flour. This will be another heavy blow for those industries. Our exports are 20 million bushels less than they were last year at this time. At present our balance of payments is in a very grave situation.
The U.S. News and World Report of November 29 states that in Canada the forest industries are pricing themselves out of the market, that eastern Canada newsprint has almost doubled in price from $147 a ton in 1970 to $285 today, and will soon be $305 a ton. The share of Canadian newsprint in
November 30, 1976

the United States market was 80 per cent in 1950, 72 per cent in 1960, and 60 per cent in 1975. An executive of Canada's Abitibi Paper explains why United States mills moved in- lower transportation costs, lower wage costs, and lower wood costs.
Wages in Canada's forest industries in a decade have swung from 7 per cent under the U.S. level to 18 per cent to 20 per cent above it. Home grown wood delivered to United States mills is at least 40 per cent cheaper than the Canadian product.
At a time when we should be trying to increase our exports, this coming year, 1977, export grain will bring in $1 billion less in foreign exchange than in 1975 or 1976. Any stoppages and interferences in respect of the export of grain tend to make the Canadian dollar devaluate overnight. It is interesting that some six months ago the Canadian Wheat Board knew the government was going to scrap the "at and east" rates so it encouraged the grain industry to construct additional storage on the west coast of Canada at farmer's expense.
The way out of our present economic difficulties can be summed up in one word, productivity. In our country it used to be thought that work was the way to wealth. Now it seems popular to think that wealth is here and it just has to be redistributed. Most of the successes of our way of life have been due to the initiative, resourcefulness, and hard work of our individual citizens. Canada was not built on a 36-hour week with all the fringe benefits. For too long now we have concentrated far too much on how to spend our wealth and not nearly enough effort on how to create it. I see nothing in this bill that will increase productivity.
The legislation in clause 8 dealing with adult training lends itself to almost any interpretation. If this country is to grow and prosper and if productivity is to increase enough to catch up with inflation, our system has to offer incentives to the individual to participate and put forth his best effort.
As I said earlier, our great agricultural industry, which this bill directly affects, does not have confidence that the Government of Canada is prepared to support a viable agriculture. Producers hesitate to put investment into land and equipment that is necessary. They see the federal government cutting back basic research. They see the flood of imported agricultural food which makes them think, and rightly so, that the government is more concerned about the well being of foreign farmers than of our own.
Clause 14 deals with the Western Grain Stabilization Plan and defers federal government payments to the plan. We have one month to go in the present calendar year in which producers can opt out of the plan. Right now 39,000 western grain farmers have opted out, or 25 per cent. The government is trying to entice them in by extending the opting-in date another month until the end of December. We have over 25 per cent who have opted out now. All the landlords are automatically excluded as are all sales over $25,000. So I doubt that half of the western grain industry will be covered by this plan. Surely better use can be found for the tax dollars than such an expensive stabilization scheme which will cost the
Restraint of Government Expenditures taxpayers of Canada something in the order of $100 million a
year.
Rules and regulations flow from government departments almost extemporaneously, without proper thought. The increasing number of reports and forms required by government puts a great deal of hardship on small business and on individuals because, unlike large organizations, they cannot afford to hire a staff of experts to cope with such harassment. Over-regulation is slowing our productivity at a time when increased productivity across our nation is the best antidote for inflation.
I can give as an example Canadian Wheat Board "Instruction to the Trade" which starts out, "Notwithstanding anything in the Canadian Grain Act," and goes on to suspend storage ticket rights of grain producers who wish to deliver to the domestic off-board feed grain market. I think the Board overstepped their authority in this case, and I intend to raise the matter in the House.
A report of the School of Business Administration at the University of Western Ontario, London, states that estimates by six large industrial firms of the cost of complying with the controls program ranged from $200,000 to $1 million per company, with thousands of firms covered by AIB controls. It is easy to see with respect to firms covered by AIB controls what the incredible cost of the program is to the Canadian economy.
Our high minimum wages have priced many students, the unskilled and older workers out of the market, and their potential is lost. What the government should be doing, Mr. Speaker, is to abolish the capital gains tax for family agricultural enterprises, and for small businesses after they have been in business for ten years, by ten per cent a year. This tax generates something less than one third of one per cent. These small businesses contribute flexibility to the economy. They work long hours and they get the work done when necessary. Canadian farmers with the help of their families have established a record of productivity per person that is hard to beat, and they do not draw unemployment pay when times are slack.
Our Minister of Agriculture is certainly consistent. He keeps bulling ahead with his supply management theories. I am looking at a report in the Vancouver Province headlined, "Whelan Wants to Oversee All Food Output". The article states:
The scope of the federal department of agriculture will be increased and strengthened before the spring budget, Agriculture Minister Eugene Whelan said Monday.
He implied that he wants a cabinet position that would give him responsibility for all food production, but said: "We have been working on a program and how would you say, probably it won't go as far as 1 want it to go."
He said his department is probalbly "the most disseminated of any department of agriculture that 1 have visited." Whelan has complained several times in the past two years that he is not responsible for all facets of agriculture.
Whelan said he wants control over all grain production-the Canadian Wheat Board is now under Transport Minister Otto Lang-and would favour the inclusion of several other agriculture programs now overseen by the department
1538

November 30, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures
of industry, trade and commerce and the department of regional economic expansion.
Whelan said that if he gets responsibility for grain production, he would put Vancouver's five grain terminals under one management authority.
He said Vancouver's grain handling problems stem from a combination of different policies by the elevator firms, and union-management squabbles.
I think western producers would want to take a long, hard look at that proposition. EIow can the minister run supply management operations when he cannot control what is coming in from overseas? The export-import laws he operates under require that producers suffer before any action is taken.
Only the federal government is responsible for international trade regulations. Support prices for any commodity cannot be divorced from international trade. Certainly no provincial government has power to set quotas or tariffs on foreign food imports, so it is only natural that producers look to Ottawa to keep their provincial programs from being eroded or erased by a flood of cheap imports. The current international controversy over offshore beef imports is a prime example and a very painful one for our beef producers. Once again I refer to the Vancouver Province of November 9, 1976. Under the headline "Marketing Boards Only Way to Protect Growers-Whelan" part of the article reads as follows:
Whelan talked to more than 130 leaders of Canada's $700 million-a-year horticultural industry for more than two hours, but his audience didn't like what it heard.
The delegates at the two-day meeting on national marketing schemes wanted a definitive statement from Whelan that Ottawa would maintain a fruit and vegetable industry and abandon a cheap, consumer-oriented food policy which relies on increasing imports from the U.S.
"We came here expecting some answers and all we got was a glowing report about different federal programs," said Nigel Taylor, a Kelowna-area orchardist and president of the Canadian Horticultural Council.
"He said nothing about our real problems and the answers we want from government," said Taylor.
Said a senior member of Whelan's department: "It was embarrassing. Whelan had to know they wanted assurances but he ducked the issue."
As I said before, the repeal of the so-called "at and east" rates will adversely affect Canada's share of world wheat exports and certainly our share of flour exports. It will probably be great for St. Lawrence ports, but it will be murder for the Maritime ports. With regard to the commission dealing with the cost of moving grain by rail, the Minister of Transport has a copy of the Snavely report, but we do not have access to it. There is no surer way to undercut a commission than to go about it as the Minister of Transport did in western Canada when he tampered with the rates on rapeseed products and as he is doing now in removing this section from the Railway Act.
We are presently facing a situation where Canada's share of world wheat exports is shrinking steadily, and there is little evidence to support an early reversal of the trend. In the ten years from 1965 to 1975 Canadian wheat exports as a percentage of total world wheat exports dropped to 14 per cent from 24 per cent. In contrast, the United States increased its share of world wheat exports to 41 per cent from 38 per cent. The situation in our flour exports was even worse. At a time when

we should be doing everything to increase exports, this bill would adversely affect grain and flour exports.
We can well ask, if farmers are expected to pay the full cost of transportation as users, why should the same rule not apply to consumers in Canada? During the past two years Canadian consumers have been subsidized for bread and pasta products to the tune of $280 million. Farmers were required to put up $64 million of that amount. The federal government turned over $216 million to the Canadian Wheat Board as partial compensation for wheat sold to Canadian millers at a floor price set by the federal government. The $64 million difference was a deduction from producers' income.
We have just seen an extraordinary marketing deal arranged by the Canadian Wheat Board. Some four million tons of wheat were turned over to the international traders. The Wheat Board, not having overseas customers for this grain, took the international trading route. Farmers are expected to pay the interest on the money which has to be used to buy the grain, and they are expected to pay for the storage. This grain can be picked up any time until next August. The carrying charges would be some 35 cents per bushel. I suspect that the Wheat Board was pressured into this extraordinary move because it cannot sell below the guaranteed initial price, which is $3. The price now at Thunder Bay is $3.25, so they are right on the line. Surely this is a most speculative deal, and one of the main reasons for setting up the Wheat Board was to stay away from these speculative operations.
We should be talking about the lack of moisture reserves across the western prairies and across the grain growing areas of the United States. It seems to me that at this stage the Government of Canada announced to the world that, given even normal precipitation next year, Canada will be hard pressed to produce an average crop. Therefore we should consider taking 100 million bushels out of our stocks and holding it, just in case, for next year. It seems to me we have too many high sounding words from the government and too few actions to correspond with them.
I commend the report of the Auditor General to this government. I suggest it fits into this bill very well. For that reason and others I am pleased to support the amendment of my colleague, the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes), which is that Bill C-19 be given a six months hoist.
I hope the government will also take into account the falling value of the Canadian dollar, which will certainly undo the work of the Anti-Inflation Board.
The Auditor General has asked that a comptroller general, a chief financial officer, be appointed to ride herd on departmental expenditures. I urge the government to appoint such an officer before asking us to pass Bill C-19.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES RESTRAINT ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this important time in Canada's history the credibility of the government is of paramount importance to every Canadian and every member of this House. It is important to give Canadians the confidence that the restraint we ask of others is practised by ourselves, confidence that all are treated fairly,
November 30, 1976

and confidence that all Canadians get full value for their tax dollar.
When the Auditor General tells us of millions of dollars paid to agents to arrange the sale of nuclear power plants to Argentina and South Korea-two countries which, in my opinion, should not have potential nuclear capability under any circumstances-the restraint practised by the government compared with that asked of the Canadian people appears as a farce.
I am going to criticize specifically clause 15 of this bill as it affects the Maritimes, and suggest an alternative approach to the government. As an alternative 1 think the time has come to examine the large, sprawling empire of government departments and agencies to determine whether the existing structure is the most efficient vehicle for serving the Canadian people, and to identify the changes required to perfect the system. I suggest we should start at square one and ask ourselves what role government should play in our society and whether we have exceeded that function, perhaps to the detriment of higher priorities.
While I have the greatest respect for every committee of this House which deals with the estimates of government, I believe the time has come to take a giant step forward in examining the total impact of government expenditures, and new systems and methods which can streamline our operation and lighten the burden on Canadian taxpayers. As a corollary to this, I believe we should examine the impact of government spending on the Canadian economy and its relationship to the inflationary spiral.
Since the Royal Commission on Government Organization, commonly called the Glassco Commission, reported in 1962, the $6'/2 billion expenditure of that year has more than tripled in the interval as shown in the main estimates before us today. In the 14 years since the Glassco Commission reported, some outstanding social legislation has been enacted, and federal government assistance to disabled and disadvantaged Canadians has improved immeasurably, both in its quality and amount. Indeed in respect of disabled people, particularly the blind, and in respect of our senior citizens I find it easy to support the proposals of my colleagues in this House for even more generous treatment. At the same time I believe we can make some real progress in identifying areas within each department of government which can and should provide a service for other departments of government, and avoid costly duplication, the tremendous expense of hiring outside professional and other services, and consulting with experts outside departments of government.
The total budgeted cost of outside consultants in all departments disclosed in the estimates is more than the total expenditures of any of the maritime provinces. I believe also that the total structure of our government has become so complex and so unwieldy that the lines of authority from the minister to those in the lower echelons are strained to the utmost.
Restraint of Government Expenditures
The ability of all departments of government to focus on any one problem in our economy, like that of regional disparity, leaves much to be desired. For example, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has expended millions of dollars in Atlantic Canada with some degree of success in building the economy of that area. As DREE takes one step forward in establishing new industries, the lack of a cohesive and progressive transportation policy erodes its effect. Clause 15 of the bill before us, repealing section 272 of the Railway Act and sentencing hundreds of maritimers to the unemployment lines, is a case in point. This case was well documented earlier in this debate by my colleagues, the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) and the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather). It is not my intention to repeat their remarks.
The total amount spent by DREE on incentive grants since its inception is considerably less than the amount projected for the Mirabel airport alone. The Auditor General's report should not be a once a year embarrassment to government. The function of this office should be a continuing service of remedial action.
In department after department of government, estimates of expenditures climb. It is imperative that every one of these expenditures receive the closest possible scrutiny, but the time allocated to our House committees to perform this function and the research facilities needed to dig into them are not sufficient to do the best possible job for the Canadian people. I feel that with the tremendous increase in the complexity of government organization since the Glassco Commission of 14 years ago, we need to examine our administrative process in the light of the vast improvements and changes that have taken place in business, accounting, policy auditing and computerization, thus ensuring that the total delivery system of government best serves the challenge the Canadian people have given us.
We know that at this time there is much evidence that the government proceeds like a whole series of separate empires. These empires often compete with each other. Sometimes they even conflict with each other. The user-pay concept for transportation suggested by clause 15 is in conflict with the use of transportation as a development tool envisaged by DREE. What a discouragement this must be for the minister of DREE! I hope he will not support this clause.
These are all reasons why it is timely to consider a new look through a new appropriately guided royal commission. What are some of the things at which we could look? I suggest the following: first, we could look at the cost of particular operations in relation to the cost of similar functions in the private sector.
Second, we could look at new approaches to accountability. The Glassco Commission tried to establish some in both the financial and personnel management fields, but the ways in which these have been adopted certainly are not working perfectly, and the demands are greater today. The Auditor General has made excellent recommendations.
80005-30'/2

November 30, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures
Third, we should look at some important aspects of personnel function. There is a good deal of evidence that labour relations in the public service are bad.
Fourth, we need to identify obsolete and outdated functions. Unless we look at something like the government every so often, things go on forever even if the need for them disappears.
Fifth, we need to identify functions which could be done as well or better in the private sector. The Glassco Commission tried to identify some of these, but not very much action resulted. It is worth another try.
Sixth, we need to look at the whole organization from the standpoint of the function it is supposed to perform and its performance in fact.
With so much change in growth in the public service, and so much change in the role of government and the character of the world around the government-the external environment-there are bound to be inadequacies and things which deserve another look so that we can feel our taxes are well spent.
If the government wants to restore credibility, to restore confidence, to really do something about restraint, regional disparities and national unity, then it should review its performance in the administration of our national affairs.
The restraint provisions in the bill before us affect every poor Canadian, and the poorest regions of Canada are hit the hardest. At the same time in another bill the banks are given extended powers to make more money through interest rates charged to Canadians who have to borrow to make ends meet. This makes the 1970's the most expensive decade in our history. The rich get richer and the poor get poorer, and the government's restraint program bites hardest in the maritimes where regional inequities are frozen in place by the operation of the Anti-Inflation Board.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES RESTRAINT ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES RESTRAINT ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to participate in the debate on Bill C-19, an act to amend or repeal certain statutes to enable restraint of government expenditures.
In the recent Speech from the Throne national unity was given top billing. The whole section on national unity, however, had to do only with the promotion of better understanding between French-speaking and English-speaking Canadians, and the official languages policy. I will not go into the subject of bilingualism or the Official Languages Act except to say that the policy of bilingualism will only work if it is perceived to be an equitable policy by all Canadians. To achieve national unity requires more than resolving the question of bilingualism. There is a feeling of alienation building up in western Canada. Westerners are concerned about the disparity in freight rates. They are concerned about Canada's energy policy.
I think it is important to understand that for many years people on the prairies were dependent primarily on agriculture.

The finding of oil and gas in Alberta, and later in Saskatchewan and Manitoba, gave rise to hopes of limited industrialization to complement our agricultural economy, which is full of uncertainties at the best of times. Finishing of beef and processing of our agricultural products at home on a large scale have not been possible because of our freight rate structure, and neither has the development of a viable agricultural implement industry. For example, it is cheaper, or just as cheap, to ship a carload of steel from Hamilton to Vancouver, as it is from Hamilton to Regina. Yet Regina is 1,200 miles closer to Hamilton.
I would like to quote from Kenneth McDonald's article which appeared in the October issue of Executive magazine:
The freight rates that penalize the west to stimulate eastern Canada's manufacturers are unchanged long after their purpose was served. The national oil policy which secured the Ontario market for western oil failed to secure the Quebec market, which would have made the whole country self-sufficient-for the specious reason that Quebec refused to yield the 1 per cent gallon advantage it derived from imported oil.
The federal politicians whose tax policies halted the western mineral exploration which would benefit all Canadians were careful not to interfere with the James Bay development which will benefit only Quebecers, and at a cost already surpassing $16 billion, when the development of Alberta's tar sands is dismissed as too costly at one fifth of that figure. In the meantime Hydro Quebec exports power to New York, tax free, at a rate of profit undreamed of by the beleagured oil companies. The provinces whose stewardship produces Quebec's annual subsidies see the money squandered on projects ranging from a superfluous airport to palatial government buildings to an Olympic site surrounded by raw sewage.
Oil and gas in the west are a non-renewable resource and will be used up by the end of this century-another 25 years. When this resource is gone, if we do not have another industrial base we could end up as have-not provinces. This is one reason why the Premier of Alberta has indicated concern about an amending formula to the British North America Act. He is concerned that changes could result in the erosion of a province's right to control its resources. I mention these problems, Mr. Speaker, first to indicate that there are problems other than bilingualism affecting national unity and, second, to give you a better understanding of some of the problems in the west.
Inflation is weakening us. The Liberal voices in government today are blaming businessmen, unions, and even the buying public, for not practising thrift and economy in their shopping habits, while they, the government, go on spending money as if it were going out of style. As the previous secretary of agriculture of the United States, Ezra Taft Benson, pointed out two or three months ago to a gathering at Cardston, Alberta and I quote:
The blame for inflation must be laid directly at the door of the federal government itself. Inflation is an increase in the nation's money supply ... an increase in the supply of money and credit.
He went on to say:
Inflation is not caused by rising prices and wages. To the contrary, rising prices and wages, as any solid economist knows, are the direct result of inflation.
It stands to reason that when the money supply is increased, all money automatically becomes less valuable. This includes our savings.
November 30, 1976

When our dollars shrink in value, businessmen naturally raise their price tags. Then their employees demand higher wages.
In a free society such as ours, only the federal government can cause inflation. And the reason it puts more money into circulation is to finance its disastrous policies of deficit spending.
As the federal government promotes more and more costly and unnecessary programs, it spends far more than it receives. So to keep in business, the government has to borrow . . . Thus, new money is created. The money supply is increased ... and ... the value of all money is reduced.
It is well to remember that continued government deficits cause inflation. Inflation is used as an excuse for ineffective price controls. Price controls lead to shortages. Artificial shortages inevitably are used as an excuse to implement rationing. When will we learn these basic economic principles?
I think we would do well to heed those remarks made in Cardston two or three months ago. I continue quoting. He suggests that Canadians could halt inflation today by-
-demanding that their government stop increasing the supply of money. It is not that the government does not know how to do it... It doesn't want to do it. Their excuse is if they stop printing money, they will plunge the nation into a recession ... or worse ... a depression precipitating an unacceptable percentage of unemployment. But the longer we delay sound action, the more it will cost our nation and its people.
My impression, Mr. Speaker, prior to coming to Ottawa as a member of parliament, was that members from all regions of Canada would meet and express their ideas in committee and would then decide on not only what is best for their constituents but what is best for the majority of Canadians. Believe me, I found out in a hurry that consensus of opinion does not prevail when we have a Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) who is committed to an over-all program of supply management as well as conducting an all-out effort to have all agricultural commodities come under the jurisdiction of federally controlled marketing boards.
I must admit I was optimistic when the present Minister of Agriculture was appointed to the agricultural portfolio. I thought to myself, at least here is a man who is agriculture-oriented. Lo and behold my assumption was not correct. The agriculture minister actually spends very little time farming. Most of his time has been spent setting up marketing boards. It is not surprising, is it, that he is not attuned to the problems facing the producer? Not only is the minister oblivious to the problems facing the producer, he must also implement government policy, which partly explains why the programs are in such a shambles. This is precisely the situation we encountered with the previous minister of agriculture, the Hon. Bud Olson of Medicine Hat. We thank the good Lord that we had such strong representation from western Canada in the House to fight so vigorously against Bill C-176. May 1 call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

subtopic: AIRPORTS-VANCOUVER INTERNATIONAL-POSSIBILITY SAND DREDGED FROM FRASER RIVER TO BE USED FOR CONSTRUCTION OF THIRD RUNWAY
AIRPORTS-VANCOUVER INTERNATIONAL-POSSIBILITY SAND DREDGED FROM FRASER RIVER TO BE USED FOR CONSTRUCTION OF THIRD RUNWAY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise again in the adjournment debate to discuss a matter which has been discussed extensively in this House. I refer to the so-called third or new runway at Vancouver International Airport.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AIRPORTS-VANCOUVER INTERNATIONAL-POSSIBILITY SAND DREDGED FROM FRASER RIVER TO BE USED FOR CONSTRUCTION OF THIRD RUNWAY
speechtext: Is it needed for Otto Lang's aircraft?

subtopic: AIRPORTS-VANCOUVER INTERNATIONAL-POSSIBILITY SAND DREDGED FROM FRASER RIVER TO BE USED FOR CONSTRUCTION OF THIRD RUNWAY
speechtext:
This runway was not necessary previously. Actually many people wonder why the Ministry of Transport decided to build a new runway. The reason was a secret very well kept by members on the government side and members of the department. Recent news stories which show how often the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) used a government aircraft to reinforce the position of his own party in western Canada indicate that the minister obviously needed a special runway for that aircraft. As a consequence, now the secret is out. We know why the Minister of Transport is going ahead with the runway. But there are some conflicting statements which have been made by the Minister of Transport, and I am not referring to other conflicting statements he made but rather to the conflicting statements he made in connection with this proposed runway.

November 30, 1976
Adjournment Debate
On October 25, as reported in Hansard at page 402, I asked the minister at what stage were the plans for the so-called new runway or third runway at Vancouver International Airport. The minister replied that certain environmental studies were seen to be necessary before any final decision was taken. He went on to say:
In the meantime, a certain amount of regular fill that is available without impact upon the waters nearby is being obtained and arranged for pre-loading in the runway area.
I put to the House that that is a clear indication that a certain amount of material, to use the minister's word "fill", was being obtained which would and could be used ultimately for construction of the runway if the decision were made to go ahead with it.
Some weeks later we discovered that a tender had been offered through the Vancouver papers on November 5 to dredge sand from the north arm of the Fraser river. I asked the Minister of Transport on November 18, as reported in Hansard at page 1,129, whether this sand was going to be used for the runway construction of which apparently, according to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc), had not been decided as yet. The minister said:
Mr. Speaker, it is sand which might be useful for that purpose if a decision to build that runway goes ahead. There is a time interval between the time the sand can be obtained and the time the necessary dredging takes place and we are therefore acquiring the sand.
Later he went on to say:
... I am told that the dredging going on and which is contemplated is required in any case. We are saving the sand in case we need it. It may be that the hon. member would be able to ask me what we will do with the sand if we do not need it for that purpose.
I submit that "that purpose" which the minister referred to was the runway. I suggested that if the construction of the runway was not decided upon, perhaps the minister could put the sand back in the river, but he did not seem to see the humour of that. However, the minister, having twice said that this sand could or would be used for the runway if it was to go ahead, is in the awkward position now of being contradicted by his officials in the city of Vancouver. I should like to quote from the Vancouver Sun of November 19 as follows:
H. A. Stevenson, regional manager of the Canadian Air Transport Administration, said Thursday that the 700,000 cubic yards to be dredged will be used for general purposes only.
He went on to say:
The area is not being dredged for a runway. We are replenishing our stock piles for general construction purposes.
The question is direct and simple, and it is time it was answered without any equivocation. The minister has said twice now that this sand would be used for a new runway, but his own officials in Vancouver have completely and utterly denied that. I want to know tonight whether the parliamentary secretary would please advise us exactly what the situation is and why his minister on two occasions would make a statement in the House which was completely contradicted by one of his own officials in Vancouver.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
