speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the hon. member's permission, I will start off with a sentence in French. Am I the grain of sand which allows the train to climb up the Rocky Mountains? I think that is exactly the role performed by the Hon. Otto Lang in the Department of Transport.

I might mention that every time the minister used the airport it was to ascertain exactly what the problems were and to discuss them with the people there.
In reply to the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) with regard to the possibility that the sand dredged from the Fraser River is contemplated for use on a new or third runway at Vancouver International Airport, I would like to say that it was on March 11, 1976, that we received program approval from Treasury Board for the acquisition of sand to be used for further construction purposes at Vancouver International Airport; and also approval in principle on the calling of tenders.
As the minister said before in reply to a question the hon. member raised in the House at that time, this sand might be useful for that purpose if a decision to build that runway goes ahead.
I would also like to add, Mr. Speaker, that for the past several years this sand has been obtained, under arrangement with relevant federal and local authorities, by dredging from the adjacent Fraser River. This is the most economical means of supply. As the supply is limited, it must be reserved and, in the past, has largely been made available on the basis of dredging programs to provide the material and to ensure the navigability of river channels.
Tenders for the dredging work closed November 25 and the three tenders received are to be reviewed December 10 by an interdepartmental committee as requested by Treasury Board.

subtopic: CAPE BRETON DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION-PAYMENTS DUE PRE-RETIRED MINERS-GOVERNMENT ACTION
CAPE BRETON DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION-PAYMENTS DUE PRE-RETIRED MINERS-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the pre-retirement leave plan, PRL, was put into effect by the Cape Breton Development Corporation following the federal government's take-over of the coal mines in Cape Breton in 1968. The thought then was that Cape Breton coal was on its way out as the private owners decided to pull out. The escalated price of oil after the formation of the OPEC oil monopoly has, of course, changed all that.
One humane, if inadequate, way of meeting the problems presented in the mid-1960's, was to pre-retire voluntarily the miners at the age of 55. Some 78 per cent accepted the offer. There was also a compulsory retirement feature for those 60 years of age. The pre-retirement benefits were to be $250 a month for married men and $200 for single men.
A major difficulty arose because ordinarily a man agreeing to the PRL plan could expect the PRL benefit plus one year of

November 30, 1976

unemployment insurance claims. The men pre-retired between 1969 and 1971, numbering some 1,500, received their unemployment insurance benefits not as a separate sum to which they were entitled but as part of their total PRL benefit. Mr. Maclnnis, who was then the member for Cape Breton-East Richmond, claimed that this was illegal and that the men were legally entitled to full PRL benefit plus UIC benefit.
When Mr. Kent became head of Devco in 1971, he separated the UIC benefit from the PRL benefit so that those who were pre-retired after 1971 received the total PRL benefit plus unemployment insurance. A group of miners representing men pre-retired between 1969 and 1971 formed a committee under the leadership of Mr. Maclnnis, which became known as the working committee for this group. This committee has, in the past, appeared before the Standing Committee on Regional Economic Expansion to present its case. Mr. Maclnnis and the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. Muir) fought their case long and hard, both in the House and in the standing committee. The Justice and Legal Affairs Committee has also studied the matter and concluded there should be a voluntary agreement between Devco and these PRL men, or else the case should be decided by the courts. The committee decided to take the Cape Breton Development Corporation to the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia-and lost the legal case. To be fair to Devco, the company offered arbitration to the men prior to the court case.
In this parliament, the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys and I have been arguing that if these men have no legal right to payment, as the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia decided, then they are morally entitled to an ex gratia payment, bonus, stipend, or whatever you wish to call it, especially in view of the increased benefits which have been granted to the PRL group by Devco since then. For example, since May 1, 1976, the PRL group through a tie-in with the Consumer Price Index are receiving the following payments: married men with a dependant, $398.51 monthly, and single men, $328.82 monthly. The hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys and 1 have been arguing that these men are entitled to a minimum of $500 for the loss of their UIC benefit-I am speaking of the men pre-retired between 1969 and 1971. This comes to a total of some $900,000.
In the past few years we had numerous meetings with the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) and Mr. Kent. Mr. Kent has appeared in all the mining towns and addressed the PRL men who belong to the pensioners union. They have agreed in writing that the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. Muir) and myself would be left to come to a compromise with the minister in charge of DREE and the head of the Cape Breton Development Corporation, Mr. Kent, on this issue. Mr. Kent, at a meeting with the men, accepted the moral obligation argument of these miners, as did the former minister of DREE. I was under the impression that the present minister also held this view.
Adjournment Debate
When Mr. Kent appeared before the committee last May 13, 1976, I questioned him and I quote from the record:
Mr. Kent, I just want to be clear about this and have it on the record. It seems to me that in the statement you have made today about the issue of the men who were pre-retired between 1969 and 1971, that you have committed the corporation to meeting the moral obligation in the form of some ex gratia payment to a larger extent than you ever did publicly before. You may disagree with me but when you appeared before the pensioned miners in Glace Bay, the pre-retirement people, and in New Waterford, after having explained the increases that they had gotten in the PRL and how you had set a basis of a decent non-contributory pension scheme that would be added, you said there were some options, such as increasing the widows' allowances, increasing the numbers of years of people who had worked in the pit and so on, as well as the option of giving some kind of payment to these men who were pre-retired between 1969 and 1971.
Do I understand from what you are saying today that these options, based upon the knowledge that has at least come from the groups in my constituency, Glace Bay and New Waterford, represent the highest priority for you in terms of helping the pre-retired people?
Mr. Kent replied as follows:
Yes, 1 think that is fair. In order that there be no danger of misunderstanding, perhaps you would allow me to restate it carefully.
What I did last fall was to describe the program as we had planned it, discussed it, and were carrying it out, with the major next step then due this July 1. I pointed out how expensive that was going to be, what had been done, what was in process of being done and, therefore, I could not say when we would be able to make any further improvements. But I committed myself very clearly to the view that further improvements are desirable when we can make them. At that time I listed the kinds of improvements that were possible and I said that as far as I was concerned I would be very much influenced by the response from the people affected as to what they felt were the priorities among those possible improvements. What I am doing today is saying that although there were some actually formal votes by some of the pensioners' clubs on the matter. .. Certainly the response that has come back, quite apart from formal votes, really has been a reaffirmation that, quite apart from this legal argument which has been such a difficult one and I think an unfortunate one for everybody, in terms of a sense of moral claim, this issue is the one which is given the highest priority by the people concerned as a whole, whether or not they are personally affected.
I recognize that and I have said that in the light of that, then certainly we would agree in giving it the highest priority among the possible improvements that we certainly hope to make as soon as possible.
On November 17, 1976, in the House of Commons, in reply to a question of mine concerning the PRL miners, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) replied as follows:
I am well aware of the situation of Cape Breton miners who had an early retirement around 1967, and I also know about the regulations which were made at that time. The hon. member also knows that the situation of those retired people has been highly improved since then, but under the circumstances my representations to the President of the Treasury Board are rather to obtain additional funds for Devco so that conditions in the mines keep on improving for the workers. Unfortunately, I am not now in a position to answer positively to the hon. member's representations. I do hope that eventually we can perhaps do so, but unfortunately the circumstances are not appropriate now.
This is, Mr. Speaker, to say the least, a highly unsatisfactory answer. One gets the impression that the minister is hoping that the lingering moral obligation will just go off into thin air. I would hate to think that the minister and the Treasury Board are punishing these people for having made a well-intentioned but tactical mistake in the past in bringing the corporation before the court.

Adjournment Debate

subtopic: CAPE BRETON DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION-PAYMENTS DUE PRE-RETIRED MINERS-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in acknowledging the sincere representations of the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan), as well as other colleagues on both sides of the House, I should like to assure the House that the department truly understands the viewpoint of the Cape Breton miners who went on early retirement in the period 1969 to 1971. I must, however, point out that in recent years there has been a very great improvement in the benefits paid to these men and to other retired employees of the Cape Breton Development Corporation. When the pre-retirement plan was started in 1969 the benefit was $250 a month. Now it is $398.50 per month.
That, however, is only a minor part of the improvement in the position of these men. At the time they were pre-retired they had nothing to look forward to in the way of a company pension plan when they reached the normal retirement age of 65. The small pension plan that there had been was being phased out as pensions under the Canada Pension Plan came into operation. This has been completely changed.
All Devco employees now receive from age 65 a non-contributory pension which, after they have had 25 years in the industry, is $133.50 a month. This pension plan is applicable in full to all those already retired as well as to those who retire in the future. More of the men who were pre-retired in the 1969-71 period are now beneficiaries of the improvement in the age 65 pension, and the others will become so. I may add that widows get the pension in the full amount.
The grievance raised by the hon. member is that when the PRL plan began it was a supplement to unemployment insurance and not a separate benefit. The result was that the men affected in 1969-71 received net payments of an average of about $500 less than they would have if the PRL amount had been paid irrespective of a man's entitlement to UIC benefits.
We all recognize the importance of $500 to these men, but I must point out that the improvement in pension benefits has already meant a great deal more in dollars than the one-time $500. That is true for all the men affected. The pension benefits, of course, also apply to people who retired early and who would otherwise in many cases have less to live on than the men affected by PRL. That is why Devco gave priority to the universal improvement in its pensions. The improvements are currently costing the corporation about $6 million a year.
Nevertheless, the corporation has made it plain that when it generates more revenue and can operate in the black it will be prepared to make further improvements and, if it is the wish of the pensioners themselves, to include in that a special recognition of the situation of the men who went on PRL in 1969-71.
However, the corporation is not yet operating in the black. It requires treasury assistance for its operations, wages, and the present level of pensions. Therefore what the hon. member is asking is a special payment from the taxpayers of a kind that I am sure we would all like for many hard-pressed people but for which it is not easy to establish a special case in times of great financial stringency.

subtopic: URBAN AFFAIRS-SACKVILLE, NOVA SCOTIA-ALLEGED CHANGE IN DEVELOPMENT PLAN BY NOVA SCOTIA HOUSING COMMISSION
URBAN AFFAIRS-SACKVILLE, NOVA SCOTIA-ALLEGED CHANGE IN DEVELOPMENT PLAN BY NOVA SCOTIA HOUSING COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some 19 years ago when I came to parliament as a rooky the concept of planning on a very large scale for municipal development was but a very small concept in the minds of those who sat in this Chamber. Since that time this rooky member has become one with 17 years' experience, with planning entering more and more into our lives, particularly government planning at the municipal level.
When I talk tonight about a municipal plan it is a plan that could only have got off the ground with the federal government providing money in the millions through CMHC. This it has done. The provincial government has provided money through the Nova Scotia Housing Commission.
Some 17 years ago when I first campaigned in the district of Sackville there were a few thousand people leaving there. Today there are more than 35,000, and this has in fact become the second or the third largest community in the province of Nova Scotia.
What brings me here this evening is the fact that I feel that when the government gets into planning surely the government has an obligation to be honest in that planning with the people. I have no fault with CMHC or its honesty and intentions. I think the answer the parliamentary secretary will give me when he replies to my complaint will be as good as the answer I received the other day from the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet). We are all on the same wave length, but I regret to suggest that the provincial body I refer to tonight is not on that same wave length. The Nova Scotia Housing Commission has shown a deplorable lack of good faith in respect of the people of the Quaker Street area of lower Sackville.
I have here a plan that is not exactly small by anyone's standards; it must be about four feet by six feet, perhaps. It is signed by the Nova Scotia Housing Commission and is given to each person who buys a particular lot in the area I am talking about. This plan shows that the land is proposed to be divided into churches, schools, parkland, and commercial areas. In short it is a modern plan. I believe the people who put this plan together did a very fine job.
You and I, Mr. Speaker, being fathers, if we moved into a new community perhaps would look first of all for the amenities which would allow our children to attend school and our -wives to shop, and our families to go to church on a Sunday morning or enjoy the other amenities such as parks. This is all set forth on the plan provided to each of the homeowners in the Quaker Crescent area. What happened was that this has all been subverted. A substantial amount of what was supposed to be used for church, school and institutional purposes has been subverted to a proposed shopping centre.
I make the argument this evening that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, in good faith, put in millions of
November 30, 1976

dollars of the money of our Canadian taxpayers into the building of homes in this area. This was money of the taxpayers in Canada from Buena Vista to Vancouver Island. Then somebody, the Nova Scotia Housing Commission, but more particularly-I will place the blame right where it goes-Mr. Regan, the Premier of Nova Scotia, and the provincial Minister of Housing, Mr. Fitzgerald, allowed that noble purpose to be prostituted by changing what in effect were guarantees in this plan. This is the way it happened.
When I raised the issue initially it made a small headline in the Mail-Star of Thursday, November 25, 1976. If we look down on page two we will find that somebody from the Nova Scotia Housing Commission, Mr. Austin-not Mr. Fitzgerald, the Minister of Housing who is only good when he is tackling federal members of parliament and not expecting them to reply back; he certainly stayed out of this fight, but he will be in it before I am through with him-the executive director of the Nova Scotia Housing Commission had this to say:
It was commission policy, Mr. Austin said, to give people purchasing lots some idea of what might be developed down the street from them-but the plans were not definitive, they were only conceptual.
It is called a legend here, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps that is what he means by it being conceptual, but in any event it certainly is as specific as anything I have ever seen. The article continues:
When Sackville Town Development Company Ltd. approached the commission with a proposal to develop the site commercially, he said, the commission was delighted, and an option was signed.
Did you ever hear anything as corrupt in all your life, Mr. Speaker? The Nova Scotia Housing Commission, a body set up by the provincial government of Nova Scotia, set forth a plan for development of a city of 30,000 or 40,000 people, and then somebody comes along and suggests that maybe instead of having a park and a school and some nice fine residential streets we could turn this into a shopping centre, and the Nova Scotia Housing Commission says "hip-hip-hooray" and tears up its guarantee to the people in that area.
I will speak until my time runs out, Mr. Speaker, so do not be afraid to set me down on the time element. I will come back on this again, and again and again. The Nova Scotia Housing Minister, Mr. Fitzgerald, is corrupt for having allowed this deal to take place, and the premier of the province is corrupt for having allowed it to take place. I hope the warden of Halifax County and the council will refuse to countenance an absolute and gross breach of faith with the people by the hundreds who bought in that community thinking they would get one kind of a deal guaranteed with their deeds, and now are being presented with something else at the whim of somebody who approached the commission with a proposal to develop the site commercially. If we allow that sort of thing to go on, God help us all.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: URBAN AFFAIRS-SACKVILLE, NOVA SCOTIA-ALLEGED CHANGE IN DEVELOPMENT PLAN BY NOVA SCOTIA HOUSING COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to state to the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) that I feel very sympathetic, and I feel he has brought this problem to us tonight in a very correct and appropriate manner.
I think it would be proper for us to review first the background of the Lower Sackville land assembly. It was the first land assembly done by the Nova Scotia Housing Commission, and since 1967 the commission has acquired approximately 1,800 acres of land in the Lower Sackville area.
The First small parcels acquired were used as sites for low cost housing, sponsored by co-operatives which required lower priced land than was available on the market in the Halifax area. By 1970 the province had begun to prepare an over-all plan for the land assembly area, but this plan has been revised many times since then. To date between 400 and 500 acres of the assembly have been developed, mostly for residential purposes.
The province elected to acquire all the land on its own account, although federal assistance could have been obtained under the National Housing Act. However, the province has received financial assistance in the form of loans under section 42 of the NHA for the design and servicing of specific parcels of land. To date these loans total $5.4 million and relate to the design and servicing of approximately 400 acres. The block of land in question is not included in this acreage but is adjacent to it.
An early preliminary plan of a section of the assembly shows this particular block as a proposed site for a school, church, shopping centre, and medium density housing. At that time it was intended that the zoning for this block be general, which would permit those uses. CMHC's records do not indicate whether the province and the city proceeded on this basis, although it is known that an alternative site for the school was subsequently selected.
In view of the several circumstances referred to, CMHC is not in a position to question the development plans of the city and province. CMHC does not know the terms and conditions under which the residential lots were sold but would expect the province, as the owner, to comply with zoning requirements and to live up to its commitments to purchasers of lots in or near this block of land. Apparently the province is satisfied that it is doing so. If the nearby residents hold evidence to the contrary, then it would seem that they should take up the matter directly with the Nova Scotia Housing Commission.
